This game is just a mess really.  Like the entire franchise it is just not interesting, nor is it a great story. It is not bad but just blatant propaganda. Honestly Baker is not as interesting as some of the other members of the unit.

First the gameplay. The game is just an on-rails shooter basically. You have chest-high walls and cover placed conveniently to fire upon enemies and push forward. The enemy AI is basically useless as they stick to their cover and move only a little bit one you kill most of their unit. Then they just move to the next cover and again... stay put awaiting death.
Missions are more like arcade levels where you can peak, wait for the enemy to peak as well and then just headshot them. That is it. Your units are only good for suppressing fire and taking enemy fire, but the moment you are spotted you are a prime target, so you dont rush in, you just flank and snipe everyone. It is extremely boring to play like this. You have no incentive to try different tactics, because for some reason the enemies are either in cover waiting or they push into the 1st cover on the other side of the shooting range and wait.... they do not attack you or try to flank you. 
They go down easily but so do you, so the segment where you go solo in a house are really annoying. As the game was not built for breach and clear type of scenarios. You still push to a knocked over cabinet, then take cover (which for some reason is almost an instant safe mode because if you crouch behind the same cover - in a way you cant see the enemy, you still get hit, but if you get into cover they magically cant hit you anymore lmao) and you proceed to shoot anyone that peeks first, rinse and repeat. Squads can die quickly so they too are useless in pushing. So in the end you end up going solo, flanking solo and sniping enemies one by one until you can push forward. Talk about boring.

Another aspect i despised is the control scheme and the way holding the right click and clicking the right click immedeately issue orders. For the life of me I do not know how many times i thought about ordering to cover fire but ended up clicking for them to go to the point up to the enemy... In the heat of battle this is awful. And best of all, THERE IS NO CANCEL ORDER BUTTON TO THELL THEM TO STAY PUT. Rainbow Six had this and that game was older.

The graphics are serviceable. Although the maps are really closed, narrow corridors that make you feel like you are replaying the same levels even from previous games. Destructable objects are few and far between but are a welcome edition.

The soundtrack and sound design is okay. I do not have much positive or negative to say. It is just there and after a while I cant even remember the soundtrack. Generic military ww2 stuff.

Now the story. As always with these overly dramatic WW2 Murican games that want to talk about the horrors of war, but also about heroes and liberators, they fall flat. Even though the cast is interesting, the overdramaticized story ruins the whole experience. I guess they tried to be like Band of Brothers and went for the cinematic approach, but they are just not fit for this. This is a movie game. So the predictable aspect of PTSD is the key point for our main character, but why so soon. It is barely 3 months after the events of the 1st game and the main character already has heavy PTSD because of private Legett.. In reality while in action your brain does not develop PTSD that quickly. It takes about 3 months to develop and that is with WAR VETERANS. Meaning people out of combat when the brain is trying to adjust to regular life. When you have time to ponder on everything due to no imminent danger and even extra free time (thinking too much) that is the point where the PTSD really kicks in. Daily life. Not in combat when there are bullets flying over your head. Every comrade that dies is a big thing, every ally is a good guy/hero, the Germans are monsters, yada yada. The obvious propaganda shlock. I can talk about war crimes from the US side regarding local women and such but here one private dies trying to save a girl he randomly kissed on a parade in a foreign country. Someone would consider that SA though. Also the part with the kid is dumb as hell. Blatant propaganda. Demonizing the enemy and making this Yankee hero look like a saint. I can go on and on but this has already gone long enough.

Thankfully we do not have more sequels from this series. The "WW2 muh freedom" fatigue was real and ended this series. For someone whose family went trough insane horrors of war and returned to destroyed cities with lots of missing friends and families, never to be seen again, starting to rebuild and go on, this game felt like an insult to real war veterans. The US could go to their warm homes and healty family and neighbors, then cry about PTSD because they had to go to Europe and shoot some small contingent of Germans while witnessing less than 1% of what horrors were done on the other parts of Europe. Also had their time with French girls and Wine from time to time.

A bummer we never got the battle of the bulge here. It's a bit of a mixed bag compared to earned in blood but still very enjoyable. A very hectic and tactical experience that is oddly unique in a shooter.

I've played through once on PC, but I have easily a couple hundred hours on console, and I just need to say, this game is a MASTERPIECE. I have never played another game in this genre or similar that is as incredible in every way. If you have any doubts at all, don't worry, PLAY IT. It's worth it, trust me.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway, developed by Gearbox Software and published by Ubisoft, represents the most ambitious and emotionally intense chapter in the Brothers in Arms trilogy. Shifting the setting from the hedgerows of Normandy to the embattled towns and highways of the Netherlands during Operation Market Garden, the game continues the story of Staff Sergeant Matt Baker and the 101st Airborne Division as they attempt to secure vital routes through enemy territory. While it retains the series’ signature emphasis on tactical squad-based combat, this installment deepens both its mechanical systems and its narrative ambition, aiming to portray not only the strategy of warfare but also its psychological toll.

At its core, Hell’s Highway remains firmly committed to the tactical philosophy that defined its predecessors. Combat revolves around suppression and flanking rather than reflex-driven gunplay. Enemy machine-gun nests and entrenched infantry are formidable threats, requiring careful coordination between Baker’s fire teams and assault squads. The player must pin enemies down with sustained fire before maneuvering a squad to attack from a vulnerable angle. This structured battlefield choreography continues to provide satisfying tactical problem-solving, and the more open urban environments of Dutch towns introduce verticality and tighter corridors that vary the formula. Buildings can be entered, streets become deadly chokepoints, and destructible cover changes firefights dynamically, reinforcing the need for adaptability.

The addition of a modernized cover system marks a significant evolution for the series. Baker can now snap to cover, lean out to fire, and move between positions with greater fluidity, giving engagements a more immediate and contemporary feel compared to the earlier titles. The health system also shifts to a regenerative “threat” mechanic, where sustained exposure to gunfire results in a red haze and eventual death, encouraging careful positioning rather than reckless advances. Although some purists preferred the harsher health rules of previous entries, the updated system helps balance realism with accessibility, smoothing out frustration without abandoning the importance of tactical caution.

One of the most striking elements of Hell’s Highway is its presentation. Built on Unreal Engine 3, the game delivers a noticeable leap in visual fidelity. Character models are more expressive, environments are richly detailed, and lighting effects give the war-torn Dutch countryside a somber atmosphere. Smoke drifts through shattered streets, artillery blasts send debris scattering, and nighttime missions are bathed in an eerie glow that heightens tension. The sound design complements the visuals with sharp weapon reports, distant explosions, and urgent shouts from squadmates that create an immersive battlefield soundscape. A controversial but memorable addition is the dynamic action camera, which slows time and shifts perspective during dramatic kills or explosions. While some players may find it stylistically intrusive, it undeniably amplifies the intensity of key moments.

Narratively, Hell’s Highway aims higher than most shooters of its era. The story does not merely recount military objectives; it delves into the psychological strain of leadership and survivor’s guilt. Baker is portrayed as a man weighed down by past decisions and haunted by earlier losses, and these emotional threads weave through the campaign’s cutscenes and quieter moments. The game explores themes of responsibility, sacrifice, and the blurred line between duty and personal anguish. Squad members are given distinct personalities and arcs, making their fates feel meaningful rather than incidental. The tone is somber and introspective, occasionally bordering on surreal in its depiction of trauma, which gives the experience a gravity that lingers long after firefights end.

Despite its strengths, the game is not flawless. Certain encounters can feel scripted, and while environments are more expansive, the overall mission structure still funnels players along fairly linear paths. The action camera and cinematic flourishes, though impactful, sometimes clash with the grounded realism the series strives for. Multiplayer modes exist but never achieve the same level of depth or acclaim as the single-player campaign, leaving the core experience centered firmly on the story-driven tactical journey. Additionally, AI behavior, while generally competent, can occasionally falter, leading to moments where squadmates hesitate or enemies react predictably.

Even with these imperfections, Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway stands as a compelling culmination of the trilogy’s vision. It refines the tactical systems that set the series apart while elevating the emotional storytelling to new heights. The portrayal of Operation Market Garden provides a fresh historical backdrop rarely explored in mainstream shooters, and the focus on the human cost of war gives the campaign resonance beyond its objectives. For players who appreciate deliberate pacing, squad coordination, and character-driven narratives within a World War II setting, the game offers a rich and immersive experience that balances strategic depth with cinematic intensity.

Rating: 9/10

Man, do I love some Brothers in Arms. This series always surprises me with its storytelling and setting, even more in this game. Thanks to great dialog and voice acting paired with outdated but still great graphics, it's able to create a nerve-wracking and tense atmosphere, very much in tune with the real events being presented. The portrayal of each episode is great with the exception of some more mellow circumstances that divert you from the importance of the situation and what's really at stake.

The gameplay always feels fresh and unique even though the level design is not the most complete or in-depth. Even then, it gives you plenty of routes to try different approaches and figure out the best solution. There are plenty of commanding sections sprinkled in with some solo situations. Here things get a bit messy with the AI, as it tries to kill itself at every step and ends up being really difficult to control and do exactly what you expect. But when it's able to follow your instructions and you reach the expected outcome, it's really rewarding. The shooting is okay; sometimes you feel like you can hit all your shots, sometimes you don't even know how you missed, but even that plays into the type of game it is, with some great mechanics implemented into this part of the game.

There's plenty of content to go through and even more after finishing the main story. The progression is fair, but towards the end of the game, missions get really hard, your character feels like it's not able to sponge as many hits as before, and you're being hit from nonexistent or non-shooting enemies.

The art and cutscenes look and feel polished and are accompanied by some great sound design. Would benefit from more weapon variety.

The whole series deserves a remaster and even a sequel.

Going into this blind I am very surprised how fun and engaging this game was. Its story, voice acting, and direction were believable for the time. And I believe Brothers In Arms is the only game that is a fps with meaningful squad mechanics, not like some top down game, no you are on the battlefield with them  You cannot defeat the enemies by yourself, you have to use your squad, they are at your command wherever you tell them to go and what enemies to concentrate fire on. When your squads and yourself fire enough at a enemy a grey circle appears indicating that the enemy has their heads down and its safe to move your squads. You got your bazooka guys, machine gun guys and the normal assault ones, and with every level having multiple flanking routes it gives a lot freedom for strategy. What really ties it together is the immersion, you really feel like a squad leader in WW2, Everyone yelling, bullets firing all over the place destroying cover, rockets launchers and tanks firing rockets, explosions going off, dirt getting kicked up, it does a really good recreating the chaos of war and its up to you to control your squads and push the line to kill the enemy. And since the ally AI will go where you tell them to, if someone gets killed its 100% your fault. The game isn't 11 hours long, but i restarted the checkpoint every time i got someone killed so i can proudly say I completed the entire game with no casualties. The game isn't perfect as it does show its age in places, you can only sprint in a straight line, the actual first person shooting ok but not good, for some reason there a few levels you are by yourself and its not that fun to play those and a couple levels near the end my ai wouldn't shot at the enemy at all, luckily quitting to menu and reloading fixes that, there are tank missions and they are okay its pretty basic. Overall I loved this game, especially when you are advancing in a area with heavy enemy resistance, and you use your strategy skills to position squads, move them when needed to and fight yourself to in the end kill everyone without suffering a single casualty on your team. Its worth the 10$ it costs but it goes on sale for 3$. Gearbox make another one of these! I would love a modern version of this

Personally, I enjoyed this latest iteration of the Brothers in Arms series by Gearbox. The graphics and gunplay were improved over the previous titles. I liked the explosion and headshot slow-mo kill cams which can get brutal/gory. The soundtrack was pretty good too. They also added a sprint feature which was fine since having something was better than having nothing.

The story telling was fairly good, emotional, and ties up some events from the previous games in the series. They also added a tank mission or two that you get to fully control one.

This game focuses more on using the new cover system that was implemented. Your accuracy is greatly improved while in cover which adds a level of sustainability so you do not die while fighting and can quick duck back to cover if needed.

Controllers ARE supported but require the in game button mapping to be reconfigured in the settings menu. I recommend erasing all the keyboard mappings and only using the controller if you want to use one. I only had to change a few of the commands to get it all working. Had 3 or 4 hangups with the controller not responding at random times but you can just pause with the [ESC] key and then un-pause with the controller to fix it.

So, why does the small Brothers in Arms series still hold a special place in my heart? Because it offers an authentic feeling and the true emotion of war – a thin thread for this genre of games, especially back when many aspects were still being tested. I can still see certain elements that feel like they were in a testing phase.

It's a shame the series stopped here. I think it would have been great to get one more farewell title, especially for us veterans who played or knew the series since its inception. But what more can you ask for? It's Ubisoft, and considering their recent releases, we're definitely not going to see a similar title or a series of this caliber anytime soon.

After the first two really solid entries in the series, came the modern hardware, but with that, also came the "Call of Duty"-sation of the game..
Pros:
-Improved gunplay
-Some of the visuals are still holding today and look spectacular
-One of the few First Person Shooter representations of the Operation Market Garden(maybe the only one, not sure about it tho)
Cons:
-The same improved gunplay, although prefered by most, makes the game the old "One-man army", and mostly renders the usage of squads useless, unless its tanks where you need to use the bazooka team
-The story turned cheesier and Hollywood-ish
-The tank gameplay: you no longer have a tank to command around, but you are the one playing as the tank, which is just a point and click section, not even 88's or other panzers being a real threat to you compared to the first two games where sending your tank just slightly awry, could mean the end of it

Concluding, from the first two games, which are revered as one of the most authentic WW2 games, with real locations and missions, to a "Call of duty"-like story of the war, with predictable moments and toned-down difficulty. Nonetheless, a solid entry, and sadly the last one in the franchise..

Very cutscene-heavy compared to the previous games, and I don't care for the linear tank levels. That aside, the gameplay takes a step forward with its destructible cover and new bazooka team. Shooting feels better too, and the contextual third-person camera makes commanding your squad notably easier.

This game aged so much more gracefully than the previous entries in the series. I can fully recommend it. Mainly due to its gameplay mechanics.

[h3] Gameplay [/h3] 

From my point of view previous entries are close to unplayable today. Gun accuracy there is so atrocious you can not take out an enemy from more than 6 meters away. Here this issue is completely gone. Especially with aim down sights weapons you often can hit an enemy on very long distance. However they still managed to balance the gameplay in such a way that player is forced to engage with squad mechanics. So while the core gameplay loop is the same - suppress enemy from front and flank from sides it feels much more natural here and not forced like in previous titles. Not like everything is perfect of course. The AI isn't the smartest so lot your squadmates deaths feel like the games fault rather than the players. Still these are minor gripes and the game is perfectly playable and enjoyable, even on harder difficulties. 


[h3] Story and setting [/h3]

The story is quite good, if you have played the previous entries. By itself it really doesn't stand on its own. The setting has been done to death at this point so it's hard to be impressed. In fact I don't know if the writers missed it during their research but there are other US divisions than 101 and 82 - many of them have done equally impressive things. The writers clearly have some talent so it would have been nice if they gave a try to idk Italy, Africa, British in Burma, or just any heck even other divisions from XVII Airborne corps.

[h3] Missions [/h3]

There are some 9 missions in the game. Most set it Neatherland countryside or small cities. Each one is fairly linear - with just enough sidepaths to enable the gameplay loop - suppressive fire and flanking. As for objectives they aren't anything special -  but given the story anything more special would feel out of place. You play as 101s not some super special forces operating deep behind enemy lines. So we get standard WW2 mix of shooting and disabling tanks/flaks. If the game was longer - currently it takes some 7 hours on harder difficulty, maybe 5 if you run on a easier ones - I guess it would get stale.  But the gameplay loop has enough substance to make even these generic levels feel interesting for the whole runtime.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

If you are in a market for WW2 shooter and don't strictly want a one man army experience give it a try. Also don't bother checking out older titles. Sure the story will suffer but the gameplay here is so much better representation of what the devs wanted to achieve it's almost uncomparable.

Stumbling upon this game in 2025 was not something I expected to do on the PC, but I'm glad it rang across my brain all the same. Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway was a great (but incomplete) leap forward for the World War 2 tactical shooter that both feels very well ahead of its time and scratches an itch that's been missing in modern gaming, while also showing a few hiccups that sadly held it back from being an all-timer.

Sergeant Matthew Baker leads a squad of 101st Airborne soldiers through Operation Market Garden, an ambitious failed attempt by the Allied forces during World War II to push through the Rhine River into Germany to end the war by Christmas 1944. It was by all accounts a disaster due to heavier-than-expected resistance by the Germans, supply shortages, bad intelligence and communication failures, and the difficulty of maintaining supply lines over a country with barely any real roads to facilitate the endeavor. One of the biggest reasons the series stands out as a whole against its competitors of its day was giving a great, comprehensive look into the tales of the 101st and their struggles with the war. Baker and his men feel human and share a sense of dread, laugh with each other, and fight like a real military unit would during a doomed invasion. Baker, Joe "Red" Hartsock, and the rest of the crew feel straight out of Band of Brothers, and it translates to the gameplay hearing their personalities shine when they shout banter at Nazis they shoot in the face.

The game's graphics and presentation is absolutely stellar even to this day. Troy Baker's first shot at video game stardom was from this series and his performance is fantastic as is the rest of the cast. The story is tight while giving great details of the battle unfolding around them in a way that feels immersive, with a beautiful Dutch landscape that range from beautiful stone cathedrals, to reddish flames of a burning countryside, to an industrial warehouse, to fields and windmills splattered with blood. The audio design is still some of the best in gaming, with Baker screaming orders to his troops with every crack of an M1 Garand or grenade hitting you right in the chest. 

Gameplay has always been one of the standouts of the series; while Medal of Honor and Call of Duty emphasized you as the gun toting badass that would punch a hole through the chest of every goose stepper near you, Brothers in Arms drags you back down to earth to remind you that you are a soldier who will quickly be Swiss-cheesed if you try to run out in the open for too long. Being a tactical shooter, you solely control your squad and let them know whether to follow you, set up in a position near cover, attack an enemy to suppress them, or now with destructible environments, blow up their cover. The friendly and enemy AI may have some hiccups (sometimes your men will refuse to find cover and get themselves shot up or run down an obviously dangerous path) but it's overall great to see in action watching an MG team spray down a small German squad for you to flank them from the sides. Each encounter goes roughly the same but it's a formula that never gets old from how you can approach it. Being a soldier who relies on your men to make it through the day is the best part of the series and one that makes you care about the soldiers you fight with.

Which is why it's a massive bummer when the game itself forgets this for some reason and makes you fight solo in many sections of the game. The game's controls and shooting mechanics are fine enough on their own, but the game is clearly made for squad based approaches. Its attempts to be a solo shooter for Baker always feel completely out of place and in terms of the plot aside from the hospital mission, nonsensical. Thankfully, the tank sections of the game control very well and feel exhilarating at times as a break from the boots on the ground action. 

I do absolutely recommend the game, and at $10 for it, the 5-6 hours it takes to complete it are a great easy thrill ride. It might be on the shorter side sadly, but the action, story, graphics, and pacing are all top notch.

I remember loving this game when it came out, and it's utterly surprising that it's holding up so well in 2025. Upon booting the game up, I was taken aback by how good the visuals look at 1440p. The only real "Ew!" moment I had was when the cutscenes ceased and gameplay started and I was met with what appeared to be 65 FOV (with no slider in the options). I was thankfully able to find a fix on the Steam forums which involved downloading a github file and setting my preferred FOV multiplier.

The truly amazing thing about this game is that it's a first person strategy game. It absolutely baffles me that other devs haven't tried to flesh out the formula Hell's Highway had going. You can get through encounters without ever firing a shot from your own gun if you are smart about how you order your fireteams (although sometimes it's fun to fire your own gun for obvious reasons).

It feels incredible to direct an assault team to pin down an enemy while you order your bazooka team to move up to a piece of cover and then direct them to blow away the destructible sandbag the enemies were hiding behind... or to instruct your MG team to leapfrog forward while you pin down enemies temporarily.

To this day, I haven't seen a smarter or more realistic suppression system in a game. For those of you who don't know, enemies have a little circle above their heads. If it's red, it means they are unsuppressed and dangerous. They will pop up and take accurate shots at you. The more you shoot at and around the enemy, the more the red circle turns grey, and when it's fully grey, the enemy is completely suppressed.

While in first person, you are able to direct multiple AI fireteams using 3D markers on the map. So let's say there is an MG in a building that you can't address. You can quite literally use third-person camera behind cover to direct your own MG to suppress the enemy MG while your bazooka team moves into range to blow up the building.

The only other game/franchise that offered this kind of gameplay was Full Spectrum Warrior. You end up using realistic tactics to deal with battlefield threats. 20+ years later and the latest Call of Duty titles still have no suppression or squad system, and you are just a rambo dummy clicking on heads and hiding when your interface is covered in tomato juice. Embarrassing.

I'd love to have seen a game that takes the Hell's Highway formula into multiplayer. Imagine a 2v2 competitive match where you and a human teammate are each directing 3-5 AI squads against human opponents who are doing the same. Imagine if there was a currency or resource system where capturing sectors allowed you to call in new weapons/squads/tanks. Would be amazing.

There is a slight bit of 2008 jank when it comes to things like low FOV, the sprinting not giving you much directional control, and the AI sometimes bugging out and getting a little lost. But the overall strategic depth you have at your command and the mostly solid execution of it dwarfs any nitpicks I have. It's an absolute travesty we haven't gotten a sequel to this game. One set in the modern era could be brilliant. Right now this game is like 5 bucks on Steam. If you like WW2 FPS and want to use your brain while playing, this is an easy buy.

[h3][b]There's Only One Way Out of Hell... And That's Through It[/b][/h3]

[b]Story 9[/b]

Returning as now Staff Sergeant Matt Baker from the first game, this installment continues the saga of the 101st Airborne Division as they parachute into Western Europe to engage the Germans from behind enemy lines. Participating in Operation Market Garden, one of the largest airborne assaults in history, Baker aims to secure critical bridges at Eindhoven, Nijmegen, and Arnhem. Alongside the 101st Airborne Reconnaissance Platoon, Baker and Red leads 3rd Squad and 2nd Squad, accompanied by original soldiers and replacements tasked with disabling 88mm cannons, securing strategic positions, and paving the way for British Army corps and logistical units. This game diverges sharply from earlier Brothers in Arms narratives by adopting a more generic Hollywood-style World War II epic tale characterized by forced characterizations, reliance on familiar war movie clichés, and an embellished story arc involving a supposedly cursed Colt M1911A1 pistol. Despite plot inconsistencies arising from fabricated casualty reports during the Battle of Bloody Gulch and abrupt changes introducing new enemy bosses, Baker’s transformation into a multifaceted leader remains compelling. His inner turmoil grappling with survivor’s guilt and PTSD adds unprecedented psychological intensity, while his bond with Red fosters an intriguing dynamic showcasing how soldiers rely on mutual trust during wartime chaos, a testament to enduring camaraderie that enriches every aspect of this gripping narrative.

[b]Gameplay 8.5[/b]

Influenced by trends in the shooter genre, particularly the success of Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare and the cinematic gameplay of Medal of Honor: Airborne, Gearbox significantly revamped the tactical squad-based gameplay, known as the "Four F's" (Find, Fix, Flank, and Finish). Key gameplay changes include a third-person cover system inspired by Gears of War, destructible environments for dynamic strategy, slow-motion headshot or grenade kills reminiscent of Sniper Elite and the health system that is similar to Uncharted, where bullets gradually turn the screen red until a hit results in instant death, encouraging players to seek cover under fire. New features also emerged, with weapons and vehicles like the Gewehr 43 and the M4A4 Sherman VC Firefly tank added to the revamped squad system. Teams like the MG Team can suppress multiple enemies, while the Bazooka Team effectively targets fortified positions and tanks. However, players can no longer use the Browning M2HB or Browning M1919A5 on moving tanks while an Assault Team rallying on foot. Though the game leans towards more linear level design, it still offers unique mission experiences set in the Netherlands, notable missions include Operation Garden, Hell's Highway, and The Rabbit Hole. The AI is improved over the older Brothers in Arms titles, showing better cover use and flanking tactics. However, there are still flaws in gameplay mechanics, such as the underwhelming Tactical Map functionality, buggy AI pathing in complex levels, dead multiplayer, and inconsistencies with weapon handling, where the M1A1 Carbine outshines the M1 Garand and Sturmgewehr 44. These issues sometimes make Hell's Highway feel less polished in its modernization efforts.

[b]Graphics 9[/b]

Although Brothers in Arms franchise may not be widely recognized for its stunning visuals, this game features some of the best first-person shooter graphics of its era. Utilizing Unreal Engine 3, it offers a cinematic experience with dynamic depth of field and consistent lighting effects that enhance both cutscenes and gameplay. The environmental details and high-quality textures effectively represent the events and locations of Operation Market Garden, while graphic portrayals of war, such as blood splatters, wounds, and realistic dismemberment, add to the visceral combat experience. The game also introduces destructive physics, allowing for a destructible environment that includes concrete buildings, sandbags, and smaller items like bottles and flower pots, which enhances immersion. Furthermore, the user interface has been improved for better visual feedback and a more user-friendly experience, facilitating command issuance and environmental interaction for a more fluid tactical experience. However, the game does have notable shortcomings that can detract from immersion; one significant issue is memory management, which may lead to glitches like missing textures during gameplay and could necessitate restarting entire chapters. Additionally, there are minor concerns, such as less appealing models for British soldiers compared to their American counterparts, inconsistent facial animations, and lip-syncing issues. While some animations effectively convey emotional weight, others can appear awkward and fail to match the intensity of the dialogue.

[b]Sounds 9.5[/b]

Gearbox is excelling with Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway's soundtrack and voice acting. The game's scores, composed by Ed Lima and Duncan Watt, evoke the intensity and emotional weight of World War II and complement the narrative themes. Five outstanding tracks are "Main Theme", "The Story So Far", "Baker's Dozen", "Eindhoven" and "Farewell is Goodbye". The dynamic sound mix adapts to the gameplay, with the music intensifying during combat and fading to silence during quieter story moments, adding depth to the experience. With Troy Baker as Matt Baker and David McGarry as Red, both reprising their roles, the voice acting is also impressive. Enriched by dialogue that explores the personalities and challenges of the squad members, the cast as a whole delivers more nuanced and emotionally engaging performances. The script's use of authentic military terms and the addition of new accents help to bring the characters and setting to life. The battle and environmental sound design in this sequel is noticeably improved, capturing realistic audio details from the roar of explosions to the ambient sounds of war.

[b]Replayability 7.5[/b]

On the topic of replayability, Hell's Highway offers fun authentic modes, cool easter eggs, Kilroys, and reconnaissance reports. But unfortunately, these things can't make up for the fact that this game has the lowest replay value of the three Brothers in Arms games; contributing factors include linear level design that makes it predictable and repetitive, a dead multiplayer mode that can't be saved by the AI Bots mod, the absence of Earned in Blood's challenging skirmish mode in this game, and the lack of the Extras mode, which includes behind-the-scenes footage, developer interviews, and the official recording of the game's soundtrack; although there are recon reports, it's still not the same as having an entire Extras filled with those things. While there are some significant improvements over its predecessor, the game doesn't fully capitalize on its potential replay value, so it doesn't quite live up to the expectations of a sequel.

[h3][b]Overall 8.7[/b][/h3]

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway offers a compelling narrative driven by Staff Sergeant Matt Baker's transformation into a multifaceted leader amidst the chaos of Operation Market Garden. The gameplay has been revamped with a third-person cover system and destructible environments, introducing new features like the Gewehr 43 and M4A4 Sherman VC Firefly tank. However, the game faces criticism for its linear level design, poor Tactical Map functionality, and inconsistent AI behavior, which undermine its polish. The soundtrack and voice acting excel in evoking the intensity and emotional weight of World War II, but the game's replay value is hindered by its predictability and lack of substantial multiplayer options.

I picked up [i]Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway[/i] as a part of a bundle. i remember long ago when I saw it on the shelves of Blockbusters with a hint of curiosity burning in my mind, but never quite enough to invest the energy into finding out.

Now that I've sank my teeth into it, I can't say that I'm impressed - especially now.

There are four twists on the traditional [b]Call Of Duty[/b] style of gameplay.
What's similar is that the game is completely linear, in a war setting, and where you mow down droves of static enemies as you progress - it's a typical corridor shooter.
What it does differently leaves a bitter taste in my mouth:

Firstly, most interestingly, it gives you command of squads to place around the battlefield to flank and suppress enemy positions. It seems rather novel at first commanding your team to get into strategic positions and move while the enemy is suppressed to catch them by surprise. There are three fundamental problems with this design: AI, Levels, and Balance. The Ai, frankly, is none too bright - and so the developers pumped numbers up and down accordingly to keep the pacing predictable - the problem is that your strike teams will be tools that you rely on to scrape by, but are not focused or decisive enough to prove to be effective tools in their own - you won't see your teams mow down enemies in the open or dispatch foes without your intervention, they're completely supplementary. An issue is that levels are designed around this suppressive fire and flanking behavior - and so where there can sometimes be either a focused and straightforward blitz in games like [b]Call Of Duty[/b] or a more methodical and open approach in other combat-centric corridor shooters like [b]Doom[/b] or even [b]Battlefield[/b], [i]Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway[/i] has each level designed around a very specific and formulaic dance. While the concepts seem fresh for the first few minutes, the pattern becomes rather drab and predictable - becoming rote and predictable in the worst way. The final straw is Balance. The entire game is designed around you ordering your units about to suppress, flank, and take cover - but the scenarios are completely carried by the player; the player is the one intended to pick off foes with headshots, rush enemy lines, pull out daring manuevers, and make the plays happen - and you feel it. The other squadmates don't deal enough damage or pick off foes efficiently enough to turn the tide, and foes spawn and react based on your position and progress, not the team's... it makes it feel like you accomplish little to nothing if you try to get your team to do all the work for you, but likewise face insurmountable difficulty if you try to play the hero like in other games. You simply have to go back and fourth between micromanaging your team and supporting them as the only competent member of the team. All in all, it feels rough - like your team members would be dead weight if the combat was not so awkward.

The other major deviation from the Call Of Duty formula, is instead of keeping players in the action and engaged with snappy cutscenes and a breakneck pace, the flow is all over the place. There are tons and tons of cutscenes and dramatic flashbacks where interpersonal connections play out like a soap opera. We're supposed to piece together what we are not explicitly told - and it's all very petty. Even bigger moments where we are supposed to feel some semblance of emotion lose their sense of tone by overplaying their heand and wallow in a quagmire of endless melodrama. There's a lot of '[i]Story[/i] in this game, but it's not worth your brain space. Worst off, the drama is not only ineffective, but it also wavers in tone - aspects of grief are contrasted by comedy, moments of levity are spiked with loss, ruminating on lost brothers is entreated to sarcastic indifference; you're expected to care and not take it too seriously, to feel emotionally invested without having a meaningful connection to anyone in the convoluted story.

To top it off, the balance is pretty bad. Enemies disregard anything and everything - and only target you with as good an accuracy as they can commit to. Shooting through walls, blind firing with pinpoint accuracy as you peek over a trench while they are suppressed by allies elsewhere, and reacting with preternatural speed to your momentary exposure. Yet, it isn't too difficult straightforward - enemies poke their domes over the top for you to pick off with rifles - but they are beefy to body shots, and weapons are painful to handle... It takes 3 body shots from an M1 Garand to put an enemy down... [b]3!![/b]. It's not even hard, it just takes a couple more clicks than usual and turns trivial bits of combat into a slog. Enemies melt you faster than a candlestick, so you have to be cautious - they aren't hard to hit, but take a few shots to put down. It's the perfect mixture of fair-but-boring. Is it balanced? Sort of. It's just not very satisfying.

Another deviation from the basics is that there are... [i]No True Setpieces[/i].
Where other games typically have a globe-trotting adventure even back to the original [b]Call Of Duty[/b] back in the 90's, [i]Brother's In Arms: Hell's Highway[/i] is more than content focusing in on one location and one setting, which becomes grating over time. While one can stomach the stagnation for a bit, it's simply too samey to hold attention. Everything is a European grassland or a European city structure. You don't see the war on the Eastern front, you don't see an African tour, you don't see different areas closer to the Mediterranean, No Japan or China or Solomon Islands - nothing. Even keeping the setting focused, the 'setpieces' within are tragically underwhelming. A Tank section may take a number of seconds to beat without complexity or difficulty - a sniper section is as straightforward and drab as any other aspect of the game. It does little to add spice to the experience, and what little it does falls flat pathetically.

Regardless of what you may expect of the game, it's particularly drab. If you're interested for the shooting aspects, it's far below average. If you're interested for the story, it's very uninteresting and far less impressive than actual war stories anyhow. If you're interested in the strategic aspects, they basically don't do much and have very weak feedback. The game, in spite of all its ambition, simply is too lackluster and dry to deliver a potent experience, even compared to more mundane and average experiences in the shooter genre such as [b]RAGE[/b], [b]Crysis[/b], or even [b]Void Bastards[/b] that all are more unique and interesting in spite of their own shortcomings while [i]Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway[i] seems to linger in an awkward space.

I didn't finish the game. I didn't have to. Nearly halfway through the core experience and I didn't want to subject myself to more of it - which is the review in and of itself:
After 3 hours, I looked at the game and said "I'd rather not have to finish this one. I want to play a game that's actually worthwhile."

~

[b]4/10[/b]
[i]Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway[/i] is a [b]Below Average[/b] game.
While it shimmers in your pocket and whispers of adventure, once you whip it out and try to use it in the field, you'll find that it was always wiser to stick with a primary that fills the role so much better.

[h3] This review is going to be of both Hell's Highway, and will also be a review for the Brother's in Arms series as a whole.[/h3] I've been playing through the BiA trilogy and have made reviews for each game after I finished them. You can go to my profile to check out my reviews for the other BiA games. Now into the actual review;

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a sequel to Road to Hill 30, and somewhat a sequel to Earned in Blood. You play as Matthew Baker in HH, and you are continuing the war to fight in WW2. The first thing you will notice about this game, is how greatly the graphics have improved since the previous 2 games. HH runs on Unreal Engine 3, and the game has some of the best graphics of its time. This is of course a large jump from the first 2 games because the graphics are so different, but the gameplay has somewhat changed as well. You can do many more things now, like running, vaulting over cover, and weapons are much more powerful. 

The gameplay is much better, and worse in so many areas. Weapons are so much better, they do more damage, and aim is much better. When you start aiming, the gun will shake for a second, and then it will stay still so you can shoot an enemy. Enemies try to flee when you or some allies flank them, and in the first 2 games, enemies rarely do this. But there are some small flaws that make the gameplay slightly worse, strategy isn't as important as it used too. In the first 2 games, the strategy focused on suppressing the enemies, and flanking the enemies. But in HH, sometimes your assault team can kill a squad before you even flank the enemies. The main thing that your allies can do now is suppress the enemies, because there are less flanks, and again, suppressing the enemy can sometimes even kill enemies too. This removes a lot of strategy from the game.

The story is alright, and adds a lot new things to the original story. The story gives more detail to many characters to the first 2 games. But other than that, most of the new characters in the story are useless, there is only the British guy who (SPOILERS)[spoiler] learnt about Kevin Legget and got Baker to share the secret about Kevin. [/spoiler] But that's the only new character who you command that is actually useful to the story. But besides the new characters, there's the plot. The locations make sense, and the timeline of all the places make sense. The story is nowhere near as good as the story of the first 2 games, the story of HH is much more of a drama. It feels like these soldiers don't care about the actual war, and it feels like the characters only care about the drama.

There are some bugs, not too many bugs, but there are a few. There was one bug I encountered once that caused my game to crash on start, but I launched the game again a day later, and it was fixed, And a few times some allies got stuck on some cover on one of the earlier missions. One time an ally got stuck behind a door because a random door appeared after the next map loaded so I had to continue with one less ally until the next map loaded. And there were smaller bugs, but I pushed through them easily. That's pretty much all of the bugs I encountered throughout my playthrough of this game. 

[h2] Now for my review for the rest of the series as a whole [/h2]

Brothers in Arms is a great series that portrays tactics and brotherhood. With heavy inspiration from Band of Brothers, it pushes original gameplay, story, and portrays history in a great way. Each game in the series has unlockables that tell real stories of valiant soldiers who fought in WW2. The best series I've ever played, and I will never regret playing these games. I never will regret even playing through the frustrating moments too. 

Now my overall review and conclusion for both Hell's Highway and Brothers in Arms as a series; the game(s) are all masterpieces, the first 2 are the best, but Hell's Highway is still a great game, and every BiA player should play Hell's Highway. You need to play the Brothers in Arms series, and you need to play Hell's Highway!

Unlike the nostalgia-drenched reviews below me, I consider this game a side step or "side-grade" to the original two Brothers In Arms games and not the true upgrade it should have been. It's average to above average. I'd still recommend it, especially to those who have already invested their time in the first two games. But wow, is it annoyingly flawed. While the first two games have this "heavy" clunkiness about them (which, truthfully, gave them some of the realistic "weight" they're known for), [i]Hell's Highway[/i] is considerably smoother and yet still couldn't escape its own form of gameplay clunkiness.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]The continuing staple of the franchise, the score was once again the easy highlight and laid the foundation for everything else. It really elevated the game as a whole.
    [*]The audio and sound effects are top notch. I appreciated the team reusing a lot of the same audio files from the first two games, for continuity's sake.
    [*]The intro cinematic was fantastic, particularly after just having finished the first two games.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Relative to the first two games, this feels like a generic shooter with Brothers In Arms mechanics attached.
    [*]The game plays out more like a Hollywood movie with oodles of melodrama. You lose your chapter-by-chapter storytelling from D-Day onward like you had in the first two games.
    [*]Considerably easier than the first two games to the point where it's honestly just faster to pick up a Kar98k and do everything yourself. You'd have never done this with [i]Road To Hill 30[/i] or [i]Earned In Blood[/i].
    [*]The cover system has been done miles better in other games. You can't blind fire over cover. You can't "snap" to cover (called "digging in") unless you're extremely close. You can't use iron sights while "dug in". You can't traverse gaps in cover while still crouched (i.e., you have to exit cover, stand up, move, then get back into cover). You can only exit cover by pressing 'S', even at odd angles.
    [*]You become nigh invincible while "dug in", but, if you wanted to switch to "soft" cover and use your iron sights? You suddenly start taking shots from over and from the side of the same exact cover.
    [*]You can pretty much only sprint in a straight line. Sprinting is controlled via the 'A' and 'D' keys and not the mouse, but it's clunky and the delay between exiting cover, starting to sprint, and trying to get back into cover means you'll die more than you should.
    [*]Slow-motion kill shots were completely unnecessary and took you out of the game.
    [*]You stay zoomed in after you reload and there's no way to disable this.
    [*]If you bump into an enemy tank, you automatically die.
    [*]One level just... randomly turns into a horror game. It's incredibly jarring to have such a genre shift mid-game.
    [*]No extras? Really? The extras in the first two games were the absolute gold standard. What a complete and utter shame those were not added in here.
[/list]

It's a difficult one, this. 

I'm saying "no," as it feels like a downgrade from the original game. To be fair, it was ages ago that I last played the original, but Hell's Highway is not a complex game. There aren't dozens of layers to it that might throw off your memory. It's a cover shooter with the notable addition of simplistic squad management and suppression. That's pretty much it. 

It's also the premise of the original. In hindsight though, there are areas where the original is clearly better than this one. For example, the tank combat in the original - a non-directly-controllable and vulnerable Stuart - is vastly superior to the invulnerable (sans any infantry cover) Sherman in Hell's Highway. 

While a matter of taste, I prefer the simpler but crisper graphics of the original Road to Hill 30’s Unreal 2 to the muddy, overshaderized Unreal 3 of Hell’s Highway. 

The AI is lacking enough to make the squad system problematic. Say, for example, that an enemy is completely suppressed by one squad and you send your second team to flank them. You’ve done everything right and should expect to win, but your guys might just wait several seconds to fire without any clear reason to. Which means they’ll suffer casualties. 

Thanks to the unreliability of your squads, it’s often easier to just play whack-a-mole with a rifle, against the inevitably appearing enemy heads. Which gets samey as fast as it sounds. This isn’t a twitch shooter. 

Having said all that, I finished the game and don’t regret it much. It’s shortish, it’s got a couple interesting scenarios, and the storyline, while slightly tough to penetrate, is at least somewhat believable. The dialogue is good enough to make it clear that they didn’t skimp on the writing team. It’s not devoid of unintentional cheese, but the good bits far outweigh the baggage. 

Still, it feels like an expansion pack, in which case it would’ve been a middle child. There’s no clear beginning or end to it, and with the downgraded (or at least unupgraded) mechanics, it doesn’t feel like the design team was motivated enough. 

PS: it doesn’t work with bluetooth headphones, at least not with mine. It’s a fairly common issue online. Fortunately I also have an optional audio cable. Otherwise the game is bug-free for me.

Masterpiece. Hell's Highway improves upon Brothers in Arms Road To Hill 30 that changed the Military shooter forever. Hell's Highway is the third game in the Brothers in Arms (BiA) series, and returns you to the character of Matt Baker.

This game is still a tactical fps at heart. Commanding your squad to take out the enemy. This entry introduces the MG and Bazooka team, along with a cover system and the ability to command 3 squads at once.
The unreal engine does a good job, with much better graphics than the other games. The use of cutscenes is also a major step up. Having Baker actually talk and react to the situation in cutscenes. The introduction of the slow mo camera also makes kills more satisfying. The story of the game continues through Operation Market Garden.

The things this game does worse than the previous entries are mainly the changes made to combat. Instead of a health bar you had to preserve throughout a mission, you now have regenerating health. This one change cripples the main formula. In previous games you had to make choices and take risks, which could result in heavy damage or losses. That hp or soldier you lost would be gone for the rest of the mission. This made you take engagements very cautiously.
In Hell's Highway you have regenerating health, so just sit there and take some pot shots, and then just go back in cover and wait for the red to dissapear. This and the fact that your weapons are much more accurate than in previous games, makes engagements much easier and frankly boring at times. your squad members also reappear if you lost them when you hit a checkpoint. This takes a lot if not all of the risk out of the combat.

Apart from the health problem, this game is a fine third entry into the series. If you've played the others, than you should play this one too. Too bad we never got a conclusion to it all...

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this series take a sudden turn downward with this game. I bought the series in a pack and played them in order of release over 3 days, and man this one was a letdown after I enjoyed the first two. 

The only reason I got through this game is because the core aspect, carried over from the 1st two games, is still good. WW2 squad based shooter is the hook, and it's still good here. Compared to the earlier games, the squads feel easier to control and I dont feel like i need to babysit their pathing/positioning as much. 
That is good, but the rest of the gameplay took a turn towards bad. While the first two games were standard MOH/COD style FPS games, Hell's Highway introduces some absolutely godawful 3rd person cover-shooter style of gameplay. Similar to games like Rainbow Six Vegas 1 and 2 (which tbh this game was probably trying to copy), out of cover it is a normal FPS. When near a piece of cover, you press a key to "enter" the cover (dig-in as the game describes it), at which point you enter a 3rd person perspective. Though I got a bit more used to it as the game went on, it never felt smooth, it generally felt very clunky and frustrating. 
Now you might say "well just dont enter the cover then, just use cover like in a normal FPS". Well dear reader I'd love to, but unfortunately the developers practically force you to use the 3rd person cover system because when you are in first person, cover just straight up doesnt work.  You can be behind a wall, getting shot at; in 1st person, you are taking damage and will die, but press the key to dig in and your cover turns on and suddenly you are impervious to the enemy. 
Next, the aiming. The previous games are known for having inaccurate weapons, the idea being that you need to use proper flanking and suppression to take down enemies, rather than superhuman precision like in say call of duty. Having played the previous games I can say that is only partly true, if you are patient and careful you can be very effective and pick off targets, but this game is on a whole other level. Weapons in this game have typical FPS accuracy; you can reliably use an M1 Garand or K98 to take down enemies with ease from long range, have the time you can even pop their heads that stick an inch or two above their cover. 
Where in the previous games using suppression and flanking was a necessity, here it is optional. You can quite easily dome every enemy in an area from the start without issuing a single order. By the latter half of the game I had pretty much forced myself to stop picking everyone off, since i wasnt using squads, the whole damn point of the game. 
Another thing, what the ♥♥♥♥ is the grenade throw in this game? The previous games you threw grenades properly, in a nice arc. In Hell's Highway your character pitches them like a baseball, a little bit downwards and very fast. It's not terrible in 1st person, but in 3rd person from cover its awful, you have to be aiming at the damn sky to throw a grenade more than 15 feet. 
Simultaneous command of infantry squads and friendly armor, one of the coolest things in the 1st two games, is gone. Instead you have 3 barebone tank missions as a british firefly. Nothing bad to say about them really. The tank levels and gameplay was extremely simple, but that also means they didnt mess it up I suppose. Main reason they are so disappointing is the comparison to the way you interacted with tanks in the previous games. 

The sound was fine, the visuals are nice. I found going into the files and changing the FOV in the previous games simple enough, but for whatever reason it just wouldnt work with this game, even following guides, so I played through this at a wonderful 60 fov which definitely didnt improve the experience. Another small annoyance, you know how CoD 2 introduced the whole regenerating health with red ♥♥♥♥ on your screen when you are wounded? This game takes it to 11; when you are injured, literally the entire ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ screen goes completely red, good lord it is obnoxious. 
 
The story was okay. The parts involving your relations with the main squad mates from the earlier titles like Red and Corrion were nice, but a whole part of this game was wasted on a moronic plot point with a character doing something extremely stupid and getting themselves killed, which btw is a great way for a developer to make me less sympathetic for a character. Some aspects of it are weird to me, like for instance you have a new squad member not present in the previous games (who is for some reason English, speaks with an accent and all? why is an english guy in the American airborne?) who for whatever reason is really invested in the truth of how 2 people died in the 1st game, even though he wasnt even in the squad, or even the same company at the time? He gives your character an ultimatum, reveal the truth or he will......why? why is he doing this, what is his investment, hello, writer, anyone? 

The game is short, I finished it in an evening, and the ending is almost laughable for how weird it is. The second to last level is a tough, climactic battle down the highway itself, ending with you defending a position as german infantry and tanks swarm you and the fields around you burn, until finally 30 corps comes to the rescue. It's even titled "Hell's Highway". 
Then the last level is a quite easy fight through some sunny dutch fields, and then the game has the last tank part, then it ends. The last bit of gameplay in the game, and you are some random tank, you arent even commanding your squad. Alright then. 

All in all, not surprised this game killed the franchise.

Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway is one of those rare games that manage to capture the realistic emotion and sentiment that true soldiers on the front line experience. The series has always followed the 502nd Parachute Infantry, 101st Airborne Division throughout their trials and tribulations of war. Revealing the soldier’s deepest thoughts, fears, and personality development.
The majority of the story revolves around Staff Sergeant Matt Baker. You spend a good portion of the start of the game being shown flashbacks of his earlier years, as well as a portion of the stories (from other games in the series) leading up to this point. This is a definite bonus, as it gives gamers who haven’t played the earlier titles a chance to understand what exactly is going on. Baker spends a lot of his time between missions reflecting on his childhood as well as fallen comrades that he’s fought alongside. Throughout Hell’s Highway, these aspects come across as genuine, not corny. With this game, Brothers in Arms continues its standing as one of the most emotionally riveting series on the market.

Band of Brothers: Hell’s Highway is an emotional rollercoaster that captures the intensity, heroism, and human cost of World War II in a way few games manage. From the opening missions to the climactic battles, the game delivers tense, realistic combat that constantly keeps you on edge, while also providing quieter, reflective moments that highlight the bonds between soldiers. Be prepared this game will tug at your heartstrings and might even make you feel like you’re “cutting onions” at times.

The game is a faithful adaptation of the HBO miniseries, translating its storytelling, characters, and emotional depth into interactive form. You step into the shoes of Easy Company during Operation Market Garden, experiencing both the chaos of battle and the human stories behind it. Dialogue, cutscenes, and character interactions are handled with care, giving the game a cinematic quality that complements the gameplay.

Combat is challenging and tactical, with an emphasis on squad-based coordination. You need to think about cover, positioning, and supporting your teammates rather than just running and gunning. The pacing of missions is excellent, alternating between intense firefights and slower, tension-building segments that enhance immersion.

Graphically and atmospherically, the game still holds up well for its age. The environments are detailed and often hauntingly beautiful, and the sound design — from distant gunfire to the cries of soldiers reinforces the tension and realism.

Overall, Band of Brothers: Hell’s Highway is a must play for fans of WWII games and historical storytelling. It successfully captures the spirit of the series, delivers compelling combat, and creates a deeply emotional experience that few games can match.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is the continuation of the Brothers In Arms series following the events that took place in Road to Hill 30 and Earned in Blood. 

If you haven't played this series, I would like to say: It is not the normal run and gun WW2 shooter. Brothers in Arms has a stellar squad command system, where you as the player are responsible for moving your teams (firing team, assault team, etc). Additionally, the game uses realistic maneuvers such as flanking your enemy with one team, while the other team is laying down suppressing fire. 

The improvements compared to the previous games are mass. The squad control component of the game sees some great additions in this title. For example, you are able to control MG teams and bazooka teams in additional to your normal firing and assault teams. Also, objectively, the game looks absolutely gorgeous in comparison to the previous titles in series. Similarly, the AI squad characters are a lot smarter in this game compared to the other games (Dont @ me). 

The gun play has increased significantly. The guns are still not accurate like the previous games, but they are not absolutely useful as they felt in the two previous games. This is mostly attributable to the improvements in technology at the time of the game's development. However, I will say that the key binding by default are kind of disgusting, but after a while, they do get more comfortable. I would recommend editing your binds to whatever feels most comfortable to you.

OH! And there is now a slow motion affect sometimes when you get a one shot headshot on an enemy or if you get a few enemies with a grenade. It is pretty cool, but sometimes it can get annoying when you are in the thick of it, and you have to slow down to watch the brains fly out of a german soldier's head.

The game's story continues right after the events of the first two games. Now, Matt Baker and his squad drop into occupied Holland during Operation: Market Garden. The story is packed with emotional scenes and a really bizarre conspiracy of Matt's silver engraved pistol that was given to him by his father. Additionally, a lot of the major plot pieces within the game are connected to past events from the previous games. With this, I would strongly recommend playing those games before playing this one. The cut scenes in this game are pretty great too. They really add to the character development. 

Speaking of character development, I think that is one of the biggest strength of series. The developers of this title really put time into making relatable characters in order for the player to get engulfed by the series. 

If you are a fan of WW2 shooters, I would definitely recommend this title for you. Furthermore, I would also recommend buying it during it a steam sale. I believe there is typically a bundle of all the games for under $15. 

It is a WW2 shooter that stands out from the saturated market because it adds a specific mechanic that many games simply cannot replicate.

I remember buying Road To Hill 30 on release day for my OG Xbox, waaaay back in the day. I was blown away by the presentation and the acting, and being able to command a squad similarly to Rainbow Six BUT IN WW2! Ever since then, I bought and played any game in the series I could get my hands on, even the mediocre Sony PSP adaption.

I remember the agonizing wait from the time Hells Highway was revealed, until it finally launched. Pouring over every article, watching every interview and development doc, painstakingly patching together all the best pre-release screenshots into a custom desktop wallpaper using Microsoft Paint. 

Needless to say, I was a die-hard fanboy of the franchise.

Hells Highway finally launched, and being a broke f***er who couldn't afford a decent PC, I bought it on Xbox 360. I even still have the little Matt Baker action figure that came with my collectors edition pre-order. I was blown away by how much the technological leap the new hardware had improved the series. The graphics were amazing, the voice acting and character designs were spot on. I was hooked. I even played the multiplayer mode for the all of 6 months it had an actual multiplayer community to play with. I've beaten the game on every difficulty, and almost had the max achievement score, minus some of the stupid multiplayer ones that were basically impossible to get after a while.

Years later, I finally built my first gaming PC, and this was one of the first games I bought on my Steam Account. I'm impressed by how well the game still holds up visually. Obviously age has made it a bit rough around the edges, and the character models don't look as good as they did through my rose-tinted goggles. But compared to other games from the same time, the art style has certainly spared it some of the ravages time has done to other games.

The simple squad command system is still serviceable and intuitive enough not to cause many problems in minute to minute gameplay. The gunplay feels as smooth as it ever did, and the killcam you get for that perfect grenade throw into a squad of squishy German soldiers is still one of the most satisfying things in any game ever. The gore effects remained unmatched for the most part until very recently, so that's a plus.

All-in-all, this game is a hell of a ride, and while it's definitely showing it's age graphically, as the old saying goes:

"They certainly don't make them like they used to."

Now if we can just get Randy Pitchford to stop dropping USB sticks full of company secrets and squirt porn in restaurants, and stop pretending like Borderlands is the only IP Gearbox owns. Maybe one day we'll see the return of Matt Baker and the rest, and get the conclusion to that over decade old cliffhanger this game ends on.

Hell's Highway is the third and final installment in the Brothers in Arms series. Being the latest, it makes significant improvements upon the gameplay without sacrificing the formula that makes these games fantastic.

The graphics are fantastic, appropriate for a game from '08, compared to prior games. The game is highly cinematic, with a plethora of cutscenes and added flavor as you get to deepen your understanding of the squad relations, Baker and his cursed Colt, and the stresses of being a squad leader.

Mechanics are vastly improved, with AI being far more intelligent, accurate, and more user-friendly controls. The game is also much easier; after each section of game, most of your squad can be completely revived before the end of the mission, without any prompting. Even going through on the hard difficulty my first run, there was little challenge, especially since my guns were a lot more accurate that previous games.

Sometimes I feel like the game takes itself too seriously, or wants more emotional investment from the player with how long and frequent the cutscenes can be. At times they are well placed and give the game great flavor, and other times they make me roll my eyes and go "we're still going on about this?"

Either way, the game has not lost any of its character from the previous two installments, and gained a great deal of playability.
It's a short campaign, with an anti-climactic end (since it was intended to have a sequel that will sadly never come) but overall a good addition to the series.

Would NOT recommend playing before the first two games.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is the third game in the Band of Brothers trilogy.
On the 17th of September, 1944, Allied Forces predominantly led by the British Army embarked on an operation into the Netherlands to open routes into Nazi Germany and finish the war by Christmas of the same year.
Things didn't go as planned, and like, 30,000 people died, with 17,000 of those casualties being on the Allies side. Whether it was over optimism, more competent contingents of the German Army, or Montgomery being a big fat baby man, a lot of theories and reasons are given as to why ♥♥♥♥ hit the fan so hard. 

You once again play as Sgt. Matthew Baker of the 101st Airborne, US Army. Taken place after the events of D-Day in Road to Hill 30 and whatever happened in Earned in Blood (I never played it). You follow Baker from day one to day eight of Operation Market Garden as he struggles to keep his men alive and also not go crazy.
By the way, Matt's going crazy.

I don't know if I didn't notice it because of the older graphics of the first game, but the voice acting in Hell's Highway feels a bit stunted to me. A lot of the time it feels like your squad members aren't actually talking to one another but more like sending voice messages to one another even though they're in person. 
Its not all the time, but when it is, its pretty weird. 

Hell's Highway also adds a third person cover system that wasn't in the first game, but was a hyper popular feature back in 2006 to 2010 or so. You spend a lot of time in it, sometimes even more time than in first person. You can go through parts of the game without using it, but there are certain points of cover that don't seem to work unless you're hugging it.
Like they need some physical contact or something after a shaky break up.

You don't really have health in HH, Baker can only take one bullet before going down. Instead the “Regenerating health” is an indicator to how close Baker is to getting shot. Its odd, to say the least, for the most part it works just fine, but I found myself still getting “shot” when I was well behind cover, and sometimes I would just flat out drop dead just because my screen got too red as I was getting behind something. 

The graphics are both better than the original 2005 game, and in some parts worse. Everyone in Baker's squad are still recognizable from facial features alone, but something always feels off. Lots of people just kind of staring off into space like they saw a ghost or saw me doing something messed up. Baker looks fine, though, but everyone else is actually pretty creepy. 

Parts of the story can also be hilariously bad at points as well. There's this one point where you have to find someone from your squad who runs off, and at no point until the end of the level does Baker try to get their attention. There is even a scene where he's literally less than ten meters away and Baker just kind of watches him run off, and later after that when he DOES call out to him, the guy just keeps running like he doesn't hear him even though it was actually pretty quiet. 
I guess you could argue that [spoiler]He was trying to get the Dutch girl to safety [/spoiler] but the safest place would be with all the big tough American guys packing heat. 

There's also this whole sub plot about Baker “Trying to be best friends with his squad instead of a leader.” But...Uh.
When? 
In the two games I played, Baker doesn't really get buddy buddy with anybody. Mostly because, in the first game he was silent in everything except for monologues and squad commands. But in the third game he's almost entirely by the books. At the start of the game he was being friendly with Red, but Red is the closest thing he has to a best friend and they were at base and everyone was being friendly with everyone. 
Who wrote this? 

Franky even tells Baker to stop trying to be his dad, but Corrion interacts with Franky more and actually gives him crap, so where did this whole “Baker is trying to be a father to me.” Thing come from? 

Gear Box Writer Mike Neumann, are you okay? 

What else can I complain about? 

Oh, you run into some British soldiers later in the game, exactly 4, outside of a tank I mean. I actually mistook them for some kind of Dutch Resistance at first. If anything they looked more like soviets then they did British. 
They were also carrying M1 Garands. I don't know how accurate that is for Operation Market Garden, but I don't think it is. 

I don't know, Hell's Highway is weird for me. It feels like the end of an era for Gearbox Software. I remember, back in 2004, when I watched a presentation for Road to Hill 30. Randy Pitchford was in it with retired US Colonel John Antal. Randy seemed really passionate about the series back then, he would go off about how everyone in the squad was unique and how cool the squad mechanics were. 
Now he's all loopy and makes me look like a functional member of society instead of a professional bum fighter.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a first-person shooter video game developed by Gearbox Software and published by Ubisoft.

Story follows the 101st Airborne Division (502nd Parachute Infantry Regiment) during Operation Market Garden in the Netherlands, with Staff Sergeant Matt Baker back as a protagonist.

Gameplay adds new features while keeping the old combat scheme from previous games.
Once again you will command teams to support you, fix fire on enemies, or attack them. 
Game adds something I wanted in previous two titles-better variety of teams. Beside Fire Team that is useful to fix enemies, and Assault Team that helps with flanking them, from time to time you get Bazooka Team that can destroy covers, or Machine Gun Team that will fix and kill enemies, especially good to fix enemy mg nests. But beware that even with better mixture of Teams, you still have to show off your commanding skills, or they will die.
While most of the time you will use 4F's (Find, fix, flank, finish) to move on and safely win combats, game mixes up with moments where there is no flanking routes so you have to fight enemies straight, where you play solo, only relying on your weapon, or where you are commanding a tank to destroy Panzers or 88's (even if tank handles like a toy car it's still enjoyable).  It's a really good way to mix up gameplay, and I like it!
Finally there is a cover system for protagonist. Always bothered me that our allies can get into cover but we can't. Now you can hide behind fences, barrels, walls, and more by simply pressing a button. And you will get some Third Person action while in cover. Beware, not everything can survive a gunfire, so be sure to think twice before making a wooden fence as your cover.
There is a new health system! When you are out of cover under enemy fire, your screen will slowly turn red, meaning you are getting suppressed by enemy fire. If you will not get into cover soon, your luck will end soon and you will get shot, ending Baker's Road to Berlin. So while it sounds and looks like regeneration system, it is not. 
"Situational Awareness" system is gone, now you have a simple map, on which you can check your enemies, allies and objectives. 
The last new feature is "Action Cam". Game will reward you after getting a nasty headshot, a grenade kill, or a bazooka blast by zooming in and going into slow mode, to show brutal death of your enemy.

There are collectibles! 
You can find and recon specific points on the map to get some lore about weapons, battles, people, and more!
Besides that you can try to find kilroys! Kilroys are inscriptions in form of graffiti, and they were quite popular in ww2. Can you find them? 

Only complain I have is difficulty. There is only "Casual" and 'Veteran", with no middle ground, which annoys me.
Of course, "Authentic" difficulty with turned off everything is back, to show you real Hell. But you will get a Medal of Honor for each of them so...is it worth it?
Also I've heard that people are annoyed by game being less realistic than previous two, where now you can from time to time just rush in and mow down enemies. It is true, game is less realistic in terms of gunplay but it's still good.
Plus it's a rather small price for better gameplay variety plus the storyline.
And storyline is amazing. About bond between squad members, trust, events that happened in two previous games, and how war affects soldiers, it's one of the, if not the best ww2 story you can get in videogames. 

Beside Singleplayer, you have Multiplayer but as you might guess already, it's dead. 

Game worked like a dream. No issues whatsoever.

Voice acting is better than in previous games, while gun sounds feel a bit reused from eariler games. Soundtrack is improved!

Trading a bit of realism for gameplay and storyline, Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is the best game from whole BiA trylogy. Better variety in combat, improved sound design, many new features plus an amazing storyline. 
9/10!  "What is it that makes a great soldier? His brain or his heart?"
