TL;DR:  Hell’s Highway remains a worthwhile game, especially at its under-$5 sale prices, with fun and refreshing core mechanics and commendable writing hampered by technical issues.

Hell’s Highway released in 2008, the sequel to 2005’s Brothers in Arms:  Road to Hill 30 and its follow up, Earned in Blood (essentially a standalone expansion pack).  The hallmark of the Brothers in Arms series has always been “authenticity” – the devs never call it “realism” – placing the focus on real squad tactics and lovingly-rendered weapons, uniforms, and locales.  While other games in the genre featured run-and-gun gameplay, scripted bot allies, and set pieces cribbed from film and TV, BiA placed the player in charge of a squad and asked them to wield it as their most powerful weapon to defeat engagements pulled directly from after-action reports and photographs; Gearbox even sent teams to Normandy to take scans and pictures on the ground of real battlefield locations for levels in Road to Hill 30 and Earned in Blood.

While the earlier games in the series were well-regarded, earning mid-80s scores on Metacritic, Hell’s Highway received more lukewarm reviews, sitting a full ten Metacritic points lower than its predecessors.  As an avid fan of RTH30 and EIB, I played Hell’s Highway on release on Xbox 360, and with rumors circulating that Brothers in Arms 4 is in the works and Hell’s Highway falling below $5 in the recent Summer Sale, I decided to pick it up again on PC.

At release, I thought much of Hell’s Highway’s tepid reception was attributable to factors outside the game itself.  World War II fatigue was setting in:  by the time HH came out in 2008, Saving Private Ryan had been on DVD for ten years; Band of Brothers, one of the game's most obvious inspirations, for seven; and even Call of Duty had abandoned World War II the year before for the grays and browns and moral ambiguity of the “modern military shooter.”  Hell’s Highway’s cover system too was already becoming a meme by the time of release, with Rainbow Six: Vegas, Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter, and Gears of War all releasing in the two years prior.  And while fatigue may have played its part, the game has some significant issues beyond what I recognized through my rose-colored fanboy glasses at the time.

Make no mistake, there is a lot to recommend about Hell’s Highway.  The core gameplay mechanic of moving your fireteams into position, suppressing enemy troops, and flanking them, remains fun and underexploited in the shooter genre.  For veterans of the earlier games, the addition of machine gun and bazooka teams is a welcome shakeup.  The graphics, even ten years on, are serviceable, and the new slo-mo moments are a nice touch, if perhaps a bit too frequent.  The story, penned by Mikey Neumann – who also wrote Road to Hill 30, Earned in Blood, and Borderlands, and is lately of FilmJoy on Youtube – is solidly crafted and has far more heart and meaning in its war-is-hell narrative than can be found in any infinite number of the Spielberg pastiches seen in other World War II shooters.  In the end, it’s a basically competent cover shooter that doesn’t quite do its extraordinary mechanical concept and writing justice.

However, Hell’s Highway also suffers from some technical problems that rightly keep it out of the pantheon of great shooters.  The controls are iffy:  keys can’t be rebound and, on mouse and keyboard at least, the squad command rings sometimes seem to have an overly-sensitive mind of their own, a quirk which caused dozens of deaths for my poor squaddies.  AI pathfinding is an issue, as it is in every game of this type, with both friend and foe needlessly exposing themselves to fire on a routine basis.  The game has its fair share of glitches too, ranging from the merely immersion-killing (many enemy responses are triggered by proximity, so don’t worry, those Germans just over the next hedgerow won’t be put on alert by the sounds of you machinegunning their friends), to the annoying (in one particularly frustrating engagement, enemies repeatedly spawned out of a coverless wheat field on my flank) to the outright gamebreaking (several times I needed to revert to a prior checkpoint because cutscenes failed to trigger, or because one of my teams wouldn’t fire at the enemy).  Last but not least, the campaign is rather short – I clocked in shy of 12 hours, even with my compulsion to reload the checkpoint every time a squadmate went down – and there is little to do after you have completed the main game (sadly, it seems community-made scenarios never materialized due to a buggy, unworkable devkit).

There are also some modifications to the classic Brothers in Arms formula that let Hell’s Highway down.  Several levels feature sections where the player is alone, separated from their squad.  While these usually help advance the plot, they also strip out the game’s highlight squad command mechanic and turn it into a vanilla cover shooter with boring stretches of pot shot exchanges.  Worse are the sections where the player is ripped out of their boots and put in command of a tank.  These armor sections offer little challenge or novelty for no discernible gain; in fact, it’s a marked regression from the prior games’ use of tanks as fireteam replacements under the player’s command, rather than standalone gameplay sections.

Perhaps the biggest gameplay difference from previous iterations is in the player’s aim.  While RTH30 and EIB both featured considerable, even excessive,  uncontrollable weapon sway, which prevented the player from reliably picking off enemies at range and forced the use of fire and maneuver to get close enough you couldn’t miss, HH gives the player deadly accuracy, especially when in cover.  On the one hand, the sway in RTH30 and EIB was often frustrating, dragging engagements out for minutes while you tried to finally tag that last German and occassionally leaving you with no tactical opiton other than charging into the teeth of German guns.  On the other, it helped make the game’s weapons feel more powerful and immersive – like you weren’t really in control of your own rifle, let alone the situation – and forced the careful application of suppression and movement.  In Hell’s Highway, the accuracy of your weapons coupled with the third person view often makes them feel weightless in comparison.  More damning, many of those tense moments of closing on a machine gun nest with your squad have been replaced by simply picking off the gunner from a distance, and I’m not sure that’s a change for the better.

Finally, the game’s finale is a misstep that has bothered me since I first played it on Xbox 360.  Hell’s Highway seems cut short, with the final checkpoint strangely and anticlimactically placing the player in a tank instead of with their squad; the preceding cutscene feels like the buildup to a tough fight in which the player will have to use all the assets at their disposal, including armor, only to instead find yourself slogging through another dull tank section that offers no challenge or excitement.  I would not be surprised at all to learn that a big full-squad finale was the original plan, only to be cut due to time pressures or the decision to make tank sections standalone.

Overall, Hell’s Highway remains a solid game ten years after release.  The writing is refreshingly good by shooter standards and the fire and maneuver gameplay mechanic remains a treat, even if the game’s problems sometimes dull the fun.  If you’re looking to try a new shooter, Hell’s Highway is a solid pick.

Hell's Highway is the definition of a good-not-great game.
The (as of 2018) last Brothers in Arms game tells a decent story, continuing the Matt Baker narrative from the previous titles, and atmospherically it shines with a solid score and good moment-to-moment play. 

Hell's Highway is let down by repetitiveness. Though the standard gameplay (moving from cover to cover, directing troops to execute flanking maneuvers on German troops and artillery) is very good, the game barely iterates on it between the first and last mission. Too many objectives are simply "destroy the enemy 88s", with the sole difference being more, rather than different, stuff to shoot in the end game compared to the start. Where the game does try to change things up, it does so with banal tank sections and lone-wolf levels, which seem out of place. I beat the campaign in about seven hours, and was for the most part pleased it was not much longer. There's little to do outside of the campaign. The port is not very good, although the game is old enough now that most newer hardware should not have much of an issue anyway.

Overall, I recommend Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway for anyone who enjoyed shows like Band of Brothers and fancies a solid WWII campaign. That said, I would wait for a sale - I paid £2.14 in a sale (75% off), and for the content available I would be wary of paying much more. Otherwise, a decent title that just about deserves a recommendation.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway; Where do I start? 
- Only realised that this game was actually on steam a few days ago. I immediately bought it just for the nostalgia, having played it when it originally released in 2008. Not expecting too much in the way of visuals and gameplay, I was pleasantly surprised at how good the game looks (considering it's 10 years old), as well as how fun the gameplay mechanics are. In BiA:HH, the suppression mechanic makes for much more tactical battles that really focus on how the player deploys his different squads and who they're targeting, making for very enjoyable gameplay if you're into a more tactical approach. Taking out enemies feels realistic, with only 1-2 shots needed to take targets down. The story of Matt Baker struggling with his PTSD alongside the gradual attrition of his unit makes for a rather compelling account, while also taking place in the lesser seen sector of the Second World War; Operation Market Garden. Overall, this game is a must-have for more tactical FPS/TPS fans, especially those who prefer WW2 games. Even if you're only buying this for the nostalgia like myself, it is well worth the £8.50 price tag for that feeling alone. However, there's one question that still needs to be answered; Where's the Battle of the Bulge based sequel Gearbox Software? The time for a Single-Player authentic and tactical WW2 shooter is ripe (especially after the awful COD:WW2) and yet, sadly, there is nothing to suggest that a sequal is coming.

[h1][b][i]Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway[/i] – Gearbox Software[/b][/h1]

Upon the completion of the final installment in Gearbox Software’s acclaimed trilogy, I have quite a lot to say. Not a lot of it is good. Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway was released on PC on October 8th, 2008, and takes the protagonists of the previous games (who for review purposes I will now name) Matt Baker and Joseph ‘Red’ Hartsock directly into Operation Market Garden, the ambitious offensive planned by the foolhardy General Montgomery to bridge a path along the Netherlands and forge a direct line straight into the German heartland past the Rhine river. Be aware that I did my first and only run-through of this game on the hardest possible difficulty, with an additional difficulty being unlocked at the end of my play.

Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway has clearly sought to elevate the Brothers in Arms foundations established in the two previous games to new heights, taking every aspect of what made up the series and presenting it on a new scale both functionally and visually. However, immensely serious changes in gameplay dynamic make the game abundantly easy even on the games hardest first time difficulty, with other functional changes impacting the way the game is played as well. Visually, the game is quite amazing at most points, Gearbox Software employs the Unreal Engine 3 to great effect, creating what is by far one of the greatest looking World War 2 action games I have played to date. But all this is hampered by a weakness in what Brothers in Arms prides itself most in: Plot. It’s these three areas that largely define what Hell’s Highway is, that is, a very different game from its predecessors. For better or (much) worse.

What I actually liked about the game, aside from the graphical enhancements:
[list]
 [*]The use of Cut-scenes far more often, with superb animation compared to the series standard, really helps the game achieve it’s initial intention of being a cinematic war movie homage, alike to Band of Brothers. They also make Brothers in Arms’  trademark employment of recurring and developing characters much easier to keep track of, something sorely missing from the previous games which lead to a lack of connection with the plot.

 [*]The addition of a cover system, including destructible cover at regular intervals, is a welcome inclusion. The functionality of the system never gave me any issues throughout the entire game and generally made command and control a bit smoother. Vaulting too, this was an addition that made too much sense not to include I presume.

 [*]Inclusion of more friendly NPCs is a great plus. Just being able to see realistic military conditions around you, with other soldiers operating along the battlefield really helps remove the feeling of emptiness that plagued the previous games. Further effects like planes and paratroopers in the sky greatly added to this as well.

 [*]Voice acting and editing has been greatly improved with this title. Conversations between characters are for the larger part much smoother, crisper and well cut this time around, once again helping with plot development. Characters are also a lot more responsive and verbally active in combat now as well.

 [*]For the larger part of this review, I am going to speaking rather negatively about the games combat functionality and changes, so here is what I appreciated the developers doing: A greater variation of fire-teams with different weapons and abilities really helped shake up gameplay at points and Hell’s Highway’s Combat Map is a marked improvement from the situational overview screen from the previous two games. The ability to command three fire teams by the end of the game was a great choice, but really could have been implemented throughout the whole game in my opinion.
[/list]
That just about covers the praises I have for this game beyond by next paragraph. I’ve saved the graphical enhancements for last as they are the most profound improvement featured in Hell’s Highway. Almost 10 years on, and the game still looks great. The characters, combat areas and weapons are all beautifully textured, with generally consistent good animation to boot. It’s really gives a remarkable addition to the game, awarding me a shred of disbelief suspension despite all the crappy aspects about this game that are to follow. Unfortunately, as it’s well acknowledged to this day, graphical improvements are not a redeemer of poor game design.

The most glaring terrible issue with Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway is its gameplay changes. It simply makes small but high impact choices across the whole game and certain missions that degrade the entire experience to a shadow of the previous two games. Accuracy in the game has been raised on all weapons, leading to a situation where 90% of the time, commanding your squad effectively or using small infantry tactics is completely unnecessary and quite often less effective than simply going ‘Call of Duty’ style and picking off hostiles at range with rifle or machine gun fire. This is compounded by the fact that by default, you’re given almost four times the ammo as you were in previous games, for all weapons, with complete resupplies made available at many points in the mission. Now while in Earned in Blood you could acquire ammo from your squad mates, this function became more difficult to use under fire when 6 sub-machine gun magazines could be expended in a matter of minutes, where any hostiles represented a much greater threat. The combination of these gameplay changes leads to the entire game being painfully easy for almost its entire run time.

The final large scale issue I had with this game was the plot. Now I’m going to not enter spoiler territory and give away any plot points, but some of the things I’m going to say will only make sense after you’ve played. It’s clear that as part of their delivering a much more up-gunned experience to top off their series, they chose to bring the plot to new heights as well. Evidently dangerous heights. Essentially, the story is delivered much more dramatic and focused than ever before, in no small part due to the improved voice acting, animations and cut-scenes. But where this all goes, ultimately falls short. A vast majority of the time, the conflict between characters and the emotional trials of the characters, primarily Matt Baker, are extremely forced. By and large, and this is difficult to back up without spoilers, the game lacks subtlety. It tried to present itself as a heightened cinematic experience, but doesn’t really bring any of the story-writing skill that one always expects even with poorly made war movies. Instead, at most points, the plot is delivered in an extremely predictable and ham-fisted way, much like the plots of many action games. But where other games can be forgiven as the plot usually serves only to advance gameplay, Hell’s Highway’s plot is very clearly central to both the core of the game and the gameplay itself, with much of it being directly attached to the plot, far more than the previous two games. I honestly felt disconnected from the plot, and would have made many changes to improve it given the chance. My lack of connection was repaired for one small moment near the end of the game, but only for a moment, and it only served to remind me what the game was sorely missing. Either way, leaves a lot to be desired.

In summary, Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway is not the game this series deserved as its sendoff, even if they put a ‘to be continued’ on the end of the game, we all know there won’t likely be a fourth game. I played the game to its conclusion for the sake of review, but otherwise it is sorely not worth the time if one is looking for an enjoyable experience akin to the original two Brothers in Arms games. Gets a 5/10 from me.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a step away from what made the series special, and after playing it, I can see why the series was canned after this one.  
 
The Brothers in Arms series prided itself with having very "authentic" gameplay, you had to employ tactics close to what was really used during WW2, like using suppressing fire and flanking. This was not perfectly implemented, and it could be a bit frustrating when your aim felt artificially crippled, but it did encourage a specific playstyle that gave a good representation of the real life tactics. Hell's Highway drops all pretenses of being "authentic" and becomes a full on gallery shooter instead.   
  
[B]Graphics & Sound[/B]

Hell's Highway is a game from 2008, and thus the graphics do look a bit dated. The screenshots on the store page feels very "generous" in their representation of the graphic, the game does not look that good. That's not to say it's a terrible looking game, most animations look quite alright, and the texture work is hardly bad. But it's showing its age.  
  
In terms of sound, the game is quite alright. Most weapons have a good kick to them, and the voice acting is relatively good. Although there should have been more voice clips recorded for the general chatter, you end up hearing the exact same lines repeated very often, and sometimes not even at appropriate moments. Like squad members complaining about the lack of movement right after they had advanced to a new piece of cover.

[B]Story[/B]
Much like the previous Brothers in Arms games, Hell's Highway really does try to tell a story, and for the most part, it does a good job at it. There's some superstition about a gun where everyone who holds it ends up killed, and this creates a bit of friction among the men. On top of that, the losses that they've suffered are starting to weigh on them, and a good chunk of the story is focused on the well being of the soldiers. And for the most part, this is quite well told, it gives you the impression that war is no game, and everyone in it suffers. And when the story puts its focus here, it's at its best. But then there are moments that get overly "cinematic", where the characters act like action heroes, and at other moments they're just acting stupid to create dramatic moments. These parts really pull down what otherwise could have been the best story of the series.  

In terms of historical authenticity, this game is... wonky. For an example, the Germans only seem to have one type of stationary/towed gun, and that's the 88. So you keep having to destroy a lot of 88s. Anyone familiar with this conflict knows how silly this is, and it's a bit like how in some games & movies, every German tank is a Tiger tank. It's just silly (in a bad way).

There's also a really out of place level where you run around in a long abandoned, ruined, burning hospital, with German soldiers calmly patrolling. Why are they there, and why don't they care about the fact that they're in a burning building? And why does this level have cheap jump-scares and music that would be at home in a horror game? It's just so jarringly out of place. 

  
[B]Gameplay[/B]
  
Oh boy, here the game suffers. As I mentioned previously, the older games in the series were trying to be relatively authentic squad level tactical shooters set during WW2, where you were forced to employ real life tactics to succeed. Suppressing and flanking was the name of the game, and you were given some somewhat artificial limitations in order to force this playstyle.    
This game removes those limitations, and also gives you regenerating health, and it completely changes the nature of the game. Where previously the most effective tactic was to suppress and flank, with just exchanging shots with enemies in cover being a slow and ineffective process, in this game your aim is very accurate, resulting in the best tactic being to sit behind cover and just waiting for the enemy to show themselves. As you've got regenerating health, taking hits is acceptable, so you can play in a very reckless way, as long as you're still in cover, or if there are not enough enemies to take you down before you start regenerating again. Your squad members are also a lot less important, and just to encourage reckless gameplay a bit more, any downed squad member will be returned as soon as you meet an objective. Where previous games encouraged you to be careful, this game encourages you to be reckless. 
The result is a game that feels like it does not know what it wants to be. Does it want to be a loud & dumb action game with fast paced combat, or a tactical shooter which forces you to play carefully and plan your every move? Well, why not an awkward compromise? The game just feels watered down, like a compromise made to appease everyone, but which pleases no-one.  

 
[b]Closing thoughts[/B]
  
While Hell's Highway does have a mostly well told story, the gameplay compromises cripples the game. I don't like to call a game "dumbed down", because most of the time when people say that, it seems to be because the developers make the game more intuitive and cuts needless clutter that just slowed down the game without adding any real depth. But this is a case where it dumbed down really fits. They removed most of what made the series special, and the result is a game that just feels watered down and unimpressive. And I completely get why they canned the series after this, despite the game ending with a "to be continued" and a part 4 being in the works.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a marked departure from the earlier games in the series, in terms of gameplay. While the basis of the game (suppress and flank) remains, the ability to "dig in", ala Gears of War, fundamentally changes how you play. It is now much easier to kill the enemy yourself, as the cover mechanic significantly changes how the gunplay works. Cover, along with a health regenerating system, renders this a very different experience to either of the preceeding games. That being said, this is still a very good game, and the best in the series in my opinion. From story telling to the raw experience of the levels, everything is more polished than either of the previous games managed to achieve.

From a technical perspective, the decision to use Unreal Engine 3 was a wise move, as the gameplay feels fluid and graphically still holds up today. Everything visual and technical has been stepped up a few notches from the previous entries in the series.

"What is it that makes a great soldier? Is it his brain? Or his heart?"

These are the words spoken by Sergeant Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division, and one of the iconic protaganists of the Brothers in Arms franchise. Brothers in Arms, as i've stated before in my previous reviews, is my favorite WW2 themed franchise; and with good reason. But Hell's Highway is it's own seperate animal. While retaining the core story, characters, and features that the series is known for, Hell's Highway takes the traditional BIA formula, and injects it with steroids. Everything the previous games did right, this game does it better. But, it's not my personal favorite in the series. That title belongs to Earned in Blood. The reason for that is because Hell's Highway has a few strange design choices, and nitpicks that hold it back from being my go-to. That being said, overall, I think Hell's Highway IS the best when compared to the rest of the franchise. Just not my favorite. But, enough beating around the bush. Let's get into it, shall we?

Story: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is set in the midst of Operation: Market Garden. The massive air and land invasion of Nazi-occupied Holland of which the end goal was to liberate the Netherlands, break through to Germany, and end the war before Christmas. However, due to the overconfidence of some Allied commanders that the Germans were on the verge of collapse lead to them overextending the Allied elements, and eventually to the failure of the operation. In Hell's Highway, you take on the role of Sgt. Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division that takes part in the airborne side of the invasion (obviously). Baker finds himself in a tough spot at the outset of the game. Due to all of the casualties taken and friends lost during D-Day, the company has taken on many new uppity replacements. Those that survived the initial invasion are obviously a bit urked by how excited the newbies are for combat, and thus, Baker, as a platoon leader, must try to convey some sense of order. After the company settles with it's compatriots, it's time for the real deal. You'll be travelling to many locations throughout Hell's Highway. From the colorful and vibrant Holland countryside, to the bombed out ruins of war-torn cities. All the while coping with the sorrow and guilt of those that we've lost thus far. Hell's Highway's story is second-to-none in the realm of WW2 shooters, even today. Rivaling that of the HBO series Band of Brothers if followed across all three installments. That should tell you all you need to know if you're asking if the story's any good.

Graphics: Hell's Highway is an absolutely beautiful game, even by today's standards. The vibrant colors, overall fidelity, and lighting are stunning when looking at the time the game was released. Visual feedback and most animations are good as well, though there are some that could do with some improvement. Overall, there's not much to complain about on the graphical side of things.

Sound: Hell's Highway's sound design is well above average, i'd say. It's a definite improvement from the previous installments, but some weapon sounds could certainly stand for some improvements. The MG-42, for example still retains that downright annoying Hollywood stock machine gun sound. It sounds more like a broken chainsaw belt than the menacing "Hitler's Buzzsaw" that we all know. But, that's more of a nitpick than anything. Voice acting is great, as always in BIA. And they actually added more explosion sounds this time around! Overall, sound design is good. If you're not a stickler for it, there's not much to hate.

Gameplay: Now we're getting into the meat and potatoes of it. Gameplay is, by far the catagory that Hell's Highway stands out in. It's been completely revamped and streamlined for 7th gen, and it's a monumental improvement from previous installments. The "feature" where your character waves his weapon around like a cracked out zombie has been completely removed, the movement system is much more fluid with the addition of a sprint function, and the ability to jump and vault over walls, and with the addition of a sticky cover system, you'll no longer have to worry about having to run all the way across an open field just to hide behind a conveniently placed rise in the dirt. Additionaly, new weapons have been added, and many have been improved. The franchise's staple feature, the squad command mode has also been reworked and streamlined to be much more useful. This combined with some greatly improved level design results in the game being fun, and makes the player feel as though they're making progress, and not just going from firefight to firefight. Overall, the gameplay in Hell's Highway's the best it's been in the franchise, hands down.

Conclusion: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a great game. And a great BIA game at that. As I said before, it's my personal belief that Hell's Highway is the best in the series from an "everything included" point of view. Just not my personal true favorite. It more than earns the title of "cult classic" in my opinion. And is one of the best WW2 shooters out there. If you're looking for gritty, emotional, blood-soaked rollercoaster of a WW2 game, you can't go wrong.

Final Score: 9/10

Hell's Highway feels a full generation away from it's predecessors - the graphics are vastly improved and the tech can finally tell the story with all the drama and tension that they've been aiming for since the beginning. 

It also feels like a new generation in terms of the fact that a lot of the gameplay has been streamlined (grenade throwing has been tightened up, thank god), and, in my opinion, these changes have made the game easier. The new appearance of OP weapons like the bazooka team and the player-controlled tank make it a cakewalk to mop up whole squads of enemies in one shot. Your Thompson is also replaced early on with a barrel-cartridge tommy gun that feels like it never runs out of ammo. You can, with relative ease, stand back and pick off enemies from afar with the new cover system that allows you to peek around corners and focus your fire, and if you do happen to flank the enemy, often they'll stand straight up and into your squadmates' gunfire, dying in seconds. All these additions detract from the immersion, and make the game feel a little more arcadey, even thought the core gamplay mechanics are nearly identical to the previous games. All in all, this game feels much more polished and fancy, but loses some of the pulse-pounding, gritty tension of knowing that even if you're prepared, bum-rushing that dug-in squad could get you killed.

The one thing this does best is make you feel. By the last levels of the game, you'll almost want to stop playing, and the push through burning wreckages and sand dunes, being harried by multiple enemy squads, will feel dreadful, but you know that you have to keep pushing through in order to complete the mission, which is exactly how the characters feel. The narrative continues the story of Matt Baker, who is experiencing some deep PTSD/mental illness. It's incredibly bleak all the way through, and centres around a specific and almost rushed-through moment in the original game, which is retroactively filled out to fantastic effect for the player, explaining the actions of some of the characters all the way through the series. There is a subplot about a cursed weapon that it also tries to retrofit, but this doesn't stick quite as well. 

So that's it - I've played all three games in the series, one after the other, in the space of a couple of weeks. This used to be my preferred game, and it's the one I've played most, but after playing them back to back, Earned in Blood is easily my favourite, and balances a quality narrative, with realistic and rewarding gameplay, a battlefield that sounds truly alive, memorable level design, and just the right level of difficulty that rewards good tactics. The original game falls on the side of being a little too clunky, and this falls on the side of being a little too streamlined, for my tastes. In saying that, because the narrative intertwines throughout the three games, you really must play all three in order to get the full effect. Clever move, Gearbox.

This is one hell of a fantastic shooter. You continue in the story of Sgt. Matt Baker a paratrooper of 101st Airborne Division. He and his men have already gone through hell in Normandy and now there is another one ahead of them: Operation Market Garden.
[b]Gameplay[/b] is fantastic, controls are easy to learn and handle. 3rd person view, utilizing a cover and issuing orders for squads under your command. Game will quickly teach you how to use tactical manouvering and suppresive fire. Forget Call of Duty, you are no supersoldier who can take out whole garrison single-handed. No. You need to rain lead down on your enemy, so they won't dare to stick their heads up. Once they are pinned, you can outflank them and finnish from the side. Especially on higher difficuilties, the game require you to think tactically. That's what I like most.
[b]Story[/b] is one of best I ever encountered. Characters are unique, while still remain ordinary troops. No stereotypes like e.g. psycho gunner, excellent sharpshooter, and demolition guy. No, no. Brothers in Arms is all about grunts, ordinary soldiers. It's about their feels, their stories. Many of your soldiers have their own backstory (sometimes linked to previeous installments in the series), they have a different level of relationship with Sgt. Baker. Some would go to fire for him, others are questioning his ability to lead them. New guys who want to prove themselves, old friends, loyal to the end. Each with great voice-acting. Warning: there will be emotions. Thanks to excellent animation of facial expressions, you can read thoughts of your men to the point, where you will truly be part of the story. You will mourn the fallen comrade, you will mourn dead civilians. Their blood will be on your hands and altough there are no choices in this game, you will feel responsible for some of your actions nonetheless. Story is something, which make this game a real gem of WWII shooters.
And here we are - the thing I don't like. After Market Garden, there was yet another hell awaiting for paratroopers of 101st and 82nd Airborne Division. The snowy, freezing hell of Ardenne forest. Yes, Battle of the Bulge, it was supposed to be a cap stone of the story of Matt Baker and his soldiers. In the end of Hell's Highway, there is a rift, there are emotions and there are questions unanswered. I want to know how will it all end. After all, Matt made it through hell. I wonder how he would handle snow. But game devolopers will never answer my prayers...

Anyway, this is a game I recommend to any and all who like historicaly acurate WWII shooters, who like great story and who like to think tactically and feel the war as a soldier, not some god-like spec op superman.

[h1] "What is it that makes a great soldier? His brain or his heart?" - Sergeant Matthew 'Matt' Baker [/h1]

[b]Introduction[/b]
In Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway you are playing as Staff Sergeant Matthew Baker also known as Matt. You are leading your men through Holland during [i][b]Operation Market Garden[/b][/i], an Operation that had the idea of punching through the German lines in order to open a highway to give a quick end to the war and be home by Christmass.
After Normandy (First 2 BiA games), Baker's platoon is folded into a brand new Reconnaissance platoon. 

[b]Gameplay[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Movement[/b] - Movement animations are great and realistic. Whether you are walking, running or getting behind cover it feels like you are really in the battlefield.

[*][b]Engaging An Enemy[/b] - Your squad has two modes of engagement. If the Squad is in stealth mod, which means the enemy didn't notice them they would move quietly, whisper and would not engage the enemy unless you order them to unless discovered your location which is when they switch to the other mod where they will open fire at engaging enemies even if you won't order them to.

[*][b]Grenades & Explosives[/b] - Your squad will throw grenades at an enemy if they are close enough. [b]The enemy will never throw a grenade at your squad, even tho they are equipped with grenades[/b], something which older games had featured which makes it odd. 

[*][b]Recoil[/b] - The recoil of the weapons in the game is as realistic as it gets with most weapons. Just enough to keep the game enjoyable but still making your life hard to get a kill on enemy that is far away from you.

[*][b]Tanks and 88s[/b] - Feels like the enemy tanks and 88s are just waiting for you to destroy them. No huge effort is in order to destroy them unlike in older games where you needed to strategise your approach to 88s and tank positions in order to take them out or you would get your ass kicked. 

[*][b]Sounds[/b] - The game has awesome sounds when it comes to the weapons and the ambient sounds that sorround you.

[*][b]Destroy Em![/b] - Plus, unlike the first two games, in this game you can actually destroy objects. For example you can destroy sorts of covers and get your enemy out in the open and kill them.
[/list]

[b]Story line[/b]
Unlike the first two games, this game has taken the cutscenes to the next level. Almost feels like you are watching a movie.The game has great writing. The cutscenes are adding a lot to the game and to the emotions you feel while playing it. Almost feels like you are there with Baker. The dialogues during combat are amusing and at the same time feel real. Unlike in other games where when your teammates die you don't feel anything because they were 'Badass', here you are connected to the characters, you care for them and you are concerned about them during battles. When a fellow team mate gets killed, it feels like someone has just kicked you in the stomach and it brings up feelings, almost to tears at some points. In addition to what I said, in this game Baker suffers from guilt as a result of the deaths of his friends during the battles in Normandy and you can see its affect on him through out the game. The locations of fights in the game are re-created real battles that took place in the real world, they were worked on by the developers team and historians to make the game more authentic and realistic.  

[b]Graphics[/b]
The game has amazing graphics. The areas that surround you in the game are just beautiful and mind blowing at the same time. The uniforms of Allied and Wehrmacht soldiers are just beautiful to look at, the weapons look authentic and more. There are beautiful locations in alot of occasions in the game.

[b]My Opinion[/b]
In my opinion the Brothers In Arms Series is the best World War 2 series to exist. Its the most authentic world war 2 series and most realistic. It has great game-play and story-line and brings a lot of features that other games don't. No other game made me care for my team like Brothers In Arms did. I am still waiting for Brothers In Arms: Battle Of The Bulge, or what ever the name of the next Brothers In Arms is going to be.

[b] Tips for game-play: [/b] 

1)Play the game without suppression bars or any other kind of miscs on your screen;
While playing with a clean screen you can enjoy the game way more than you thought you could. Playing with a clean screen gives you the feeling you are really there in the battlefield, ordering your men.

*You will need to remember where you placed each squad and what's the role of each firing team when you order them to move because it won't tell you which firing team you chose on the screen. You might wanna know who are the soldiers of each team before you order them around so in the battlefield you will remember by that which squad is located where and move them around correctly.

*You will need to keep an eye on your fire, yeah I know hammering the enemy is fun but when you don't know how much bullets you have left in the magazine or if you have extra bullets if at all you might run into some trouble in a battle - yeah running out of bullets in-front of a German firing squad is not a great idea nor fun.

2) Play the game on authentic. Playing the Brothers In Arms series on Authentic gives you the real feeling of the battlefield. It gives you the best out of this game. Every small move, decision or order can be critical in a battle. It also disables all I said above(miscs, etc) on default because of the exact same reasons I pointed out earlier. You need to be super strategic and careful when you move your men and yourself. Stay in the open for to long and you might find yourself dead, injured or losing men. 

Thanks for reading my review.

I was in the mood for a world war 2 shooter, since nowadays those are surprisingly rare. I read reviews on Steam and Metacritic to see what was popular and Hell's Highway came up.

After beating the game I am still not entirely sure if the game deserves a recommendation or not.

For starters, the game has some glaring errors in historical accuracy, such as German 88's firing at Sherman tanks at point blank range and failing to penetrate or a single such Sherman tank rolling through hundreds of men, tanks and 88's (for some reason there are no other antitank guns in this game, just the 88 anti-air -guns) with ease. 

The graphics (originally designed for the Xbox 360) are obviously dated, with character models warping and distorting uncomfortably and facial animation all but missing entirely. The voice acting is lackluster to say the least, ambients sounds are often missing, weapons sound muted and dull and even the music seems to be oddly off-key in few points (though this part might just be my lack of knowledge showing through). All in all, the game's audiovisual presentation is pretty terrible. Even the ragdoll physics are glitchy as heck (I shot a german soldier in the head and he jumped 50 meters in the air as he died)!

So far, then, this seems like a no-brainer: an ugly game with bad audiovisual design through and through.

And then we get to the gameplay, and here I find myself intrigued. You are acting as a squad leader for most of the game, and that means you cannot just charge the enemy Call of Duty -style, but have to order around your fireteams (up to three at a time, ranging from machine gun team to base of fire team to bazooka team to assault team), setting them up in cover, assigning them targets to suppress and maneuvering them to outflank the enemy. The levels offer a sometimes surprising amount of freedom in how much you can maneuver and the system feels surprisingly good most of the time. I especially enjoyed the frantic tension of emerging into a new area only to observe a german squad marching across a field, ordering my men into position and then watching the enemy spread out into cover as the shooting starts. The enemy AI is also surprisingly good, acting surprised where appropriate, falling back and regrouping into better positions as they are overrun our outflanked and generally putting up a good fight.

And then the game shoots itself in the foot again. Several times I had the AI completely glitch out, with my machinegun team or bazooka team simply freezing in place and refusing to move, getting stuck in walls or cover and such. The game hands you a sniper rifle on a few occasions, which immediately results in you, single handedly, gunning down literally dozens of germans within a minute or two, utterly breaking any immersion the game might have had so far. The tone of the game is all over the place, and then, in the end credits, comes the final straw. The story ends on a minor cliffhanger with "To Be Continued" -emblazoned on the screen. This game came out in 2008. I played it in 2016. There are no sequels, and likely never will be.

Game Over.

This game is pretty fun and not as much of a b-list game, as I expected for the price.  This is a fairly linear, old-school WW2 shooter, with a cool squad factor.  Beware of have far away you are and the path a squad might take though.  I've had them basically commit suicide by running through enemy lines, rather than behind something.

You are part of a glider team that lands in Holland sometime after D-day, and basically have to move forward and  clear out a lot of Nazis.  There is also an interesting back-story that unfolds, involving the main character's engraved .45 pistol.

As far as the game mechanics they are pretty much what you would expect with standard motions, weapons and shooting.  Strangely, there is no jumping, except for valting over a cover item.  If the game  recognizes an item as cover you can also vault it.

As far as the cover,  pressing Q benind a solid wall or other solid item like vehicles will put you in  in a temporary 3rd person cover mode, and you are crouched behind the cover item.  Using the arrows allows you to  move behind the cover or lean out to shoot.  This mode also give you a a much finer cross-hair for aiming, and a much steadier aim.   This is kind of  cool, but also has a  drawback, as you can' t control how far you lean out (or up if behind a wall).  So when shooting from cover you have to expose yourself to multiple enemies.   The method is to take fire until the view is starting to get pretty red, then go back into cover before dying-- and hopefully killing a Nazi or two in the process.  This is a little lame and would be much better if you could lean just enough to sight in on a single enemy, depending on the positioning.

Another really lame thing is that when sprinting you can't change direction very much with the mouse.  You can use A and D keys to kind of swerve--, but you basically have to stop sprinting to make a normal turn.  This is very weird to get used to, and I can't imagine what the  developers were thinking. Another weirdness is that while in cover and being flanked it is easy to get "stuck" to the cover.  The only way to get off is to move directly backwards, and that is easy to  forget when under fire.

Still, in spite of these negatives, this is a pretty fun game, especially for the price.

If you think you would like an old-school, ww2, squad shooter with a decent story then skip a fast-food lunch and you'll have the cash for this game.  Bon Appetit.

It's a good game - a strong example of a squad-based shooter. You control the position and focus of 1-3 fireteams, edging your way through battlefields to flank enemies and progress through linear levels. It encourages you to leverage your fireteams because your own weapons are unreliable to the extreme - on par with Counter-strike accuracy. Bullets spray for no particular reason, shots that are dead-on don't always register, and enemies take many shots to take down. While that's frustrating, it highlights that you are not a pure badass. Sure you may mow down hundreds of enemies in a playthrough, but ultimately it tries to knock you down to size with it's iffy gun mechanics - you need to use your squad to succeed. And while it is frustrating to not be rewarded for your own skill, i can understand that sloppy controls make you rely on your squad more.

It also seems to want to be Band of Brothers, the TV show. The game spends an enormous amount of time showing wooden characters (some of which are obviously derived from Band of Brothers characters, one of which even shares a voice actor) talking to each other about the war and each other. It spins narratives about cursed guns and lost loves which have exactly nothing to do with the game. The first ten minutes (not an exaggeration) is a series of unskippable cutscenes that awkwardly introduce a set of characters which it clearly wants you to be invested in. It keeps introducing new characters who have small quirks and different voice actors, but whom you really don't care about. When it kills off or maims a character, you're clearly expected to care, but there's no *reason* to care; the gameplay (controlling the position and focus of 1-3 fireteams) is identical no matter which characters are involved, and you're aways given replacements who are exactly as capable. Cutscene after cutscene is used, even with "shaky-cam" effects and close-ups of expressionless faces. It's all the more frustrating because this came out a year after Bioshock, a game which is almost purely story-driven, uses the same engine, and yet falls into none of the gameplay or storytelling pitfalls that this game does.

Ultimately, it's a fun game that executes a squad shooter very well, despite the flaws. I'd recommend it if you're certain you want a squad shooter, and wouldn't recommend it for any other reason.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway was an amazing experience and an example on what modern military shooters should do nowadays, yes, looking at you, Call of Duty and Battlefield. At thing which bugs me about modern shooters is that every single one of them has its focus on the repetitive multiplayer where as today most of them play essentially the same, just as the campaign. 

We need more games like Hell's Highway which are not glorifying war but show the human side the soldiers have instead of how many times they can yell "♥♥♥♥ YEAH, AMERICA!" while pulling out the flamethrower to "burn them, burn them all!!!"

The men you fight along in Hell's Highway feel human and just as in the older Brother's in Arms games, the main focus lies in the single player. If you want to buy this game for a killstreak loaded multi player to "pwn scrubs", you are wrong here.

A roughly about 10 hours long campaign (I played on Veteran difficulty)  will keep you motivated with a nice tactical component to command different squads such as the MG squad or the assault team as Matthew Baker, to surpress the enemy and use the element of surprise to flank clueless and somtimes dumb acting enemy soldiers. The commanding barely gets old and as you hop around different hubs of the hot areas during the war. Those range from wide fields to close battles in troubled cities and villages as well as asylums and collapsed buildings.

The thing which does get a little repetitive are the objectives you have to achieve using those methods of commanding. Most of the time you find yourself having to destroy 88 cannons and sometimes drive a tank around in which you are mostly safe even on the higher difficulties. Really annoying did those things only become in the end to me, as the game finally came to a closing, during the last hour of gameplay. The story itself kept motivating as protagonist Matthew Baker's mind started to crumble and he realized more and more and war is insanity. 
The "To Be Continued" in the end was a huge bummer to me though, especially because Ubisoft doesn't seem to care at all about this amazing series which could definetly standout amongst "Call of Boredom" or the recent development of the"Battlefail" games.

It doesn't need amazing graphics to make a good game. While Brothers in Arms may looked fine back in the day it is quite outdated for the modern standards. Second to none facial animations, horrible lip-synching at times but nice destructability of cover and physical correctness of the debris look damn fine as well as gore and ragdoll of fallen enemy soldiers. 
Also the sound design is great and as the bullets fly over your head  in cover and the enemies speaking correct German, which is a rare thing to see to be honest. The atmosphere is really great and makes you feel as if this was an episode of the critically acclaimed "Band of Brothers"-TV show. The developers really did a great job in capturing an unique and equally terrifying experience.

Overall Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a technically and gameplay wise far from flawless but also an unique and tactical game which definetly gets a recommendation for me, even if solely for the atmosphere and the long campaign.

Grab this game if you are sick of modern shooters and/or glorification of war.

A worthy sequel to the first two Brothers in Arms games. There's a very emotional story here that makes the events of the previous games come full circle, and one which the game flaunts with well choreographed cinematics. The gameplay feels like a next-gen evolution of Brothers in Arms in all the right ways. Cover, destructible levels, multi-squad command, air recon, the map replacing SA view, sprinting, and the kill-cam all fit right into Brothers in Arms and don't make the game lose its identity at all. The levels are bigger and better than anything seen before, and the enemy AI is as great as it ever was. The graphics, unlike the first two BiA games, actually stand the test of time thanks to vibrant, colorful levels and tasteful use of visual effects and bump mapping, unlike most early 7th gen video games. Another issue is that weapon sway when aiming is not in this game, except for a second immediately after the player aims. Other than that, this game is an improvement over the originals in every way.

Hell's Highway is a game with a solid gameplay experience, an interesting narrative, and some glaring faults.

As a direct sequel to the first game in the Brothers in Arms series Hell's Highway follows newly-promoted Staff Sergeant Matt Baker and his unit  through the Netherlands during Operation Market Garden. Baker's sanity wanes due to the contention of his men, rumors of a haunted pistol, and the memories of friends lost. 

The combat in HH holds to the tradition of the earlier titles in the series, while adding additional squads and features. Flanking and diversionary tactics are vital, as running into the open while an enemy fires upon Baker or his squad will result in a quick death.

However, Hell's Highway is a game that needs some fixing to enjoy. For anyone like myself who gets headaches or feels sick at a lower field of view, here's different methods of how to counter the horrid default setting.


--------------
Method 1: 
A simple binding to toggle the fov. This will change the fov when pressed, but will zoom out cutscenes, break sniper scopes, and disable zooming in when aiming.

Go to your "Documents\My Games\BIA Hells Highway\SumacGame\Config" folder and open "SumacInput.ini" in a text editor. 
under the"[Engine.PlayerInput]" section add the following.

Bindings=(Name="KEY",Command="fov DESIREDFOV",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)


Method 2: 
Changing the action of the zoom hold command to change the fov. The fov will lower when aiming to zoom in, then zoom out to your desired standard fov on release. This will also zoom out cutscenes and break sniper scopes. I suggest a zoom fov of 60, and a standard fov of 100.

Under "[Engine.InputActionDefinition]" in SumacInput.ini look for the line that starts with "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias...".
Change the line to, "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias=".ZOOMHOLD",Names=("Zoom"),Command="ZoomIn | fov DESIREDZOOMFOV | OnRelease ZoomOut | OnRelease DESIRED DEFAULT FOV")"

Other tips:
Creating a bind similar to the bind shown in method 1 set to "fov 63" will set cutscenes close to what they look like normally.

In the "[SystemSettings]" section of "SumacEngine.ini" you can pump up the graphics. I suggest setting "EnableHighPolyChars=False" to "True" and fiddling around with the MSAA.

Let me get this out of the way. Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is one of the best WW2 shooters I've ever played. There, I said it. Why is that you ask? It takes everything good about the first two and amps them up times ten. While the sound design, voice acting and ability to control your fire teams are the same (and still very good), graphics, level design, gunplay, and story are all much MUCH improved. The battlefield moves from France to Holland as your crew including Matt Baker and Joe Hartsock and boy, does it show. Instead of the same boring grassy humps, you'll fight in, around and through beautifully detailed farms, churches and bombed out cities. The fire fights are intense and the guns aim much better. A third person cover mechanic was also added giving you greater flexibility to kill the enemy and command your troops. Is it perfedtion? No. The cut scenes run a little long and the last mission is somewhat anticlimactic compared to some of the buzzsaws you run through earlier in the game. Since a recap of the first two games is included I would actually skip the first two BiA games because Hell's Highway is such a quantum leap for the series. I cannot recommend this game enough. I got the whole series for around $13 (it's been as low as $10) and this one alone was worth the price of admission.

The whole squad control thing didnt interest me at first, but the way you control your 1-3 units is just a two button execution. One to toggle between the teams and one to execute a order which are dynamic depending on what you are looking at. If you aim at cover, they move there, if you aim at enemies they shoot and if they are close enough they will use hand granades as well. 

Suppress, advance, flank and kill is the most common tactic. Every enemy has a icon over their general location which makes giving orders easy. While the enemy icon is red, they are a threat and can easly shoot you. If the icon are gray, they are supressed and you have a easier time advancing... and so on.

The gameplay is great, fun and works fine. The story is trying to be like the HBO series Band of Brothers, but considering the shorter time a game has to tell such a story it becomes very cheesy.

I would recommend it if it goes on sale again.

Hell's Highway continues the BiA series and updates the game's engine, but still offers the familiar feel of the previous games' squad mechanics. Hell's Highway is a worthwhile tactical-FPS game that really puts you into some of the battles of WWII while furthering the story of Baker and his dozen.

pretty graphics very immersive. Oddest of the series, has a ghost level which I think is a first for a WW2 squad based shooter. Tanks are a joke to control and rather lose the what makes BIA interesting which is the squad based stuff and focus on suppression. Guns all sound good but bigger stuff sounds better BAR's and 30 cal sound partiularly good. M1s less so. Focuses on allied failure market garden which is rare. Lots of focus on mental health of solders and gives a fair representaton of combat stress. Best in the series by a mile, pretty dated but still has it moment when it looks good.

This game is intense. You battle through hell and blood, you lose many friends along the way, You use every last bullet you can get to put nice and safe in the enemy's head. When you get a head shot it goes in slow motion. The graphics are amazing. Control your squad Baker. Good Luck Soldier! (Controls are easier on ps3)

I highly recommend the Brothers in Arms series, especially Hell’s Highway. It’s incredibly cinematic.

There is an element of squad-based controls, but the way that BiA does it makes things extremely simple. All you have to do is right click to tell your squad to go somewhere or do something. Nothing like Rainbow 6… I hate Rainbow 6.

I am a WWII game buff so this obviously fit my criteria.  This is a worthy successor to the prior BIA installments.  It has a different sort of gameplay (i.e. squad based) than any other FPS WWII games which makes it unique.  Its squad control gameplay has limitations but also has advantages and the change of pace can be refreshing.  I recommend this for WWII FPS buffs.

Although not as good as COD 2, this is still a nice addition to the BIA series. The Unreal Engine 3 still shines, and some gameplay issues have been fixed (like shooting right at the target through iron sights and shots fly everywhere but near you sights). Even though sometimes you will probably think the story rips too much from the Saving Private Ryan wannabes, it's still worth playing if you love the BIA series.

First, this game uses an early build of UE3. and it shows; in the explosions. Everything Else is Fantastically unique. Tweaks have been made to the shooting mechanics to make it easier to hit a target over the previous two titles. The story starts out as a stereotypical Death rewind scenario to perpetuate the story,this is common in MOH games, but in Gearbox fashion the end is not as you'd expect, nor is the actual opening sequence. This is a Great game and, if it has to be, a Great finish to this franchise story arc. Also must be played in succesion from the last two in a short timeframe.

9/10
